title: Rachel Ruysch: Nature Into Art. By RobertSchindler, BerndEbert, and Anna C.Knaap (eds.), Boston: MFA Publications, 2024. 247 pp., $55.00 (hardcover). ISBN: 9780878468997, 0878468994
abstract: One would have to be deeply cynical not to be enchanted by the visually stunning exhibition Rachel Ruysch: Nature into Art. Glancing across galleries painted in tones of green and shades of mauve and pink ranging from pale lilac to dark peony, Ruysch's heavy cabbage roses and bright red opium poppies beckon, enveloping visitors in a luxurious atmosphere one can almost (or, in Toledo, actually) smell. Ruysch was one of the best-known artists of the Baroque in her time; the exquisiteness of her flower still lifes was acknowledged from the moment she first started painting them, in the early 1680s. In recent years, her paintings have been included in group exhibitions on women, still lifes and nature, and early modern Netherlandish art. However unlikely it may seem, Rachel Ruysch: Nature Into Art is the first significant monographic exhibition devoted to the artist in more than 300 years. The exhibition opened at the Alta Pinakothek Munich on 26 November 2024, from where it travelled to the Toledo Museum of Art, in Ohio (April to July 2025) and to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (August to December 2025). The catalogue that accompanies the exhibition contains the only comprehensive scholarly research on the artist since Marianne Berardi's 1998 unpublished (although publicly available) doctoral dissertation, from which the exhibition derives its title. This review concerns the exhibition at all three venues and the catalogue, published by MFA Publications.1 The exhibition is timely. The urgency of environmental devastation and climate concerns have prompted several major museums to present exhibitions on flora and fauna and the art of nature. Decades of insistence on better gender representation have jolted museums into prioritizing exhibitions featuring women artists.2 Nature Into Art meets the moment. It distinguishes itself from the other recent excellent exhibitions by bringing together a broad range of perspectives, as set out below. Curated by Bernd Ebert (AP), Robert Schindler (TMA) and Anna C. Knaap (MFA), the exhibition rests on a curatorial scaffolding of four thematic pillars (the names of which vary slightly across venues): An Auspicious Beginning, which explores Ruysch's evolution as a young artist; The Two Sisters, which features a visual conversation between Rachel and her younger sister, Anna, who was also a talented artist; Art, Nature, and Science, which sets the pursuit of the knowledge of flora and fauna and the embrace of empiricism as a contextual backdrop for the world in which Ruysch's art came into being; and Fame and Fortune, which consists of an overview of Ruysch's high-ranking patrons and of her success as one of the best-selling artists of her time. A core group of approximately thirty-five paintings by Ruysch traveled to each location, with others appearing at some of the venues only. A portrait of Ruysch at work by Michiel van Musscher in collaboration with Ruysch, introducing her as a confident artist, featured proudly at all three venues (Figure 1), on display for the first time since its acquisition by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Yet, the three iterations of the exhibition varied considerably from each other, not only in size (with the AP edition being the largest and the MFA's the smallest), with respect to the selection of works on display, with different approaches to exhibition design, but also in terms of focus. In Munich, Ebert placed the emphasis on the Elector Palatine's patronage of Ruysch, a decision which enabled the museum to highlight the strengths of German collections and the artist's connections to the country, which go back at least as far as 1708, when the Elector Palatine Johann Wilhelm, high-ranking in the Holy Roman Empire and son-in-law of Cosimo III de’ Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, named Ruysch court painter. Set against burgundy walls, paintings including Bouquet of Flowers from 1708 (Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen München), with its vibrant green praying mantis, invite close inspection. A portrait of Ruysch with her husband Juriaen Pool and their son Jan Willem (named in honour of the Elector), believed to be a collaboration by Ruysch and Pool, anchors this section and underscores the significance of the patronage for the artist. Particularly compelling is a case containing a large medallion of Johann Wilhelm, like the one his namesake wears around his neck in the family portrait, and a letter from Ruysch dated 1715, in which she described a painting intended for the Elector as filled with ‘strange and rare flowers’. These objects complement the paintings and are helpful in conveying the deep appreciation the Elector had for Ruysch—and vice versa. In contrast, the intersection of art and science was key to understanding Ruysch's work at the MFA. Occupying three galleries out of the exhibition's five, arrangements of mounted insects recalling colourful mosaics, dried plant specimens, cases with oversized books and works on paper intermingled with paintings to produce a dynamic display. As the eye travelled from specimens to illustrations, one could not help trying to locate the various insects and flowers in the paintings—a Baroque version of Where's Waldo with a Hercules beetle. The first gallery drew attention to the significance of Ruysch's upbringing, together with her sister Anna, in the world of wonder created by their father, the celebrated anatomist Frederik Ruysch. The second gallery foregrounded the network of botanical and entomological artists active in Amsterdam at the same time as Ruysch, including Maria Sibylla Merian, Alida Withoos and Herman Henstenburg. Although she almost certainly would have known at least some of these artists, this is a leap that is not made explicitly in the gallery nor in the catalogue. The third gallery, also the largest, was conceived as the centrepiece of the exhibition, with its display of Ruysch's illustrations of plants non-native to Western Europe. Based on the work of Charles C. Davis (professor of biology at Harvard University and curator of the Harvard University Herbaria), a map and a video convey the wide reach of the regents and caretakers of the Amsterdam botanical garden (then known as the hortus medicus) in obtaining specimens from Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Consequently, the focus of the MFA's installation was in sharp distinction to the approach at the AP, which situated Frederik Ruysch and the evolution of early modern natural history in a gallery that stood physically separated from the others, which arguably undermined the role of science in Ruysch's artistic practice. Unintentionally, however, Boston's attention to art and science had the converse effect of shifting the visitor's attention away from Ruysch as an artist of extraordinary talent. With fewer paintings on display than in Munich but more than in Boston, the exhibition design in Toledo featured a gallery layout that naturally guided the visitor through a narrative that began with Ruysch's early paintings, not unlike at the AP, set in conversation with those who influenced her, directly and indirectly, including her teacher Willem van Aelst and (near-) contemporaries such as Otto Marseus van Schrieck, Jan Davidsz. De Heem and Maria van Oosterwijck. In a competition that pits the young Ruysch against her mentors and predecessors—searching for the most realistic morning glory, the liveliest poppy, the most dynamic ornamental grass—it seems obvious that Ruysch is destined to surpass them all. As at the AP and the MFA, visitors to the TMA were treated to drawings by Ruysch's contemporaries, wet and dry specimens, as well as large, illustrated books. It was only here, however, that extra emphasis was given to the Surinam toad, which carries and hatches its eggs on its back. The toad was a rarity at the end of the seventeenth century in Amsterdam, engaging the study and fascination of experts and curieux alike, from Frederik Ruysch and polymath Nicolaas Witsen, among others. Toledo was the only location to display a drawing of the Surinam toad by Ruysch, which Schindler discovered in the archives of the Royal Society in London. Schindler's find is significant in a number of ways. The drawing, dating to c. 1688, is the only one securely attributed to Ruysch and one of the earliest representations of the toad in Western Europe, pre-dating Maria Sibylla Merian's by at least twelve years. It is a near-perfect match for a painting of the Surinam toad by Ruysch dated 1690 (Musée du Grand Siècle, Saint-Cloud), confirming that Ruysch relied on drawings in creating the compositions of at least some of her paintings, a practice that is not surprising but for which no evidence had previously been located. Furthermore, the presence of the drawing in the archives of the Royal Society, where it most likely accompanied a letter to the Society sent by Witsen, who was a member, offers further support for the participation of Ruysch in the networks connecting empirical science and natural history in late seventeenth-century Amsterdam. Emerging from a close encounter with the Surinam toad, a visitor then walked into the world of the elite patrons that supported Ruysch from an early time, the most significant of which, of course, was the Elector. As in Munich and Boston, the family portrait of Ruysch with Pool and their son took pride of place. Here, the chronological approach worked particularly well, as the period of time spanning the patronage of the Elector (who passed away in 1716, before Ruysch's last painting for him could be delivered) coincided with the peak of Ruysch's experimentation with complex compositions that included a wide number of species non-native to Western Europe (as noted by Davis in his catalogue essay), thereby linking the galleries intellectually as well as physically. At all three venues, the exhibition closed with the small paintings that Ruysch produced in her old age. These canvases, unlike the almost bombastic compositions such as the Nelson-Atkins Museum painting (see Figure 2), are subdued, in a softer colour palette. They feature simple compositions of local flowers. Dating from the 1730s and 1740s, these paintings reflect the aesthetic tendencies of the rococo. Importantly, they display the sensibilities of an artist who is proudly able to carry on doing what she loves—as the paintings Ruysch inscribed with her age attest. The intimate scale of these works creates a quiet bond between artist and viewer, a sentiment which is also evoked by a small portrait of Ruysch in ink by Aert Schouman dated 1749, one year before her death. Unlike the portrait by Van Musscher (Figure 1), the artist shown here is old, with sunken, wrinkled cheeks (Figure 3). The attributes that accompany the depiction of the artist include brushes, grapes and peaches, and the medallion of Johann Wilhelm—a reminder, if one was needed, that Ruysch remained an acclaimed artist to the end. The most engaging and innovative aspect of the exhibition across all venues was the exploration of the fluid relationship between art, nature and science, a topic that has received increasing scholarly attention over the past decade. Bringing this field of inquiry to the public is important; as Eric Jorink and Bart Ramakers (2011) noted, ‘in the early modern era the contemporary Latin terms ars and scientia were complementary rather than opposites, covering a spectrum of meanings such as skill, experience and knowledge’ such that ‘the meanings of the words are often interchangeable’. Interestingly, and perhaps surprisingly, the topics of imperial botany (which some scholars have termed biopiracy) and colonization were only directly addressed at the MFA and the TMA, the latter unfortunately in an area situated at the exit of the exhibition, which disconnected these practices from the beautiful art that they made possible. Although the AP installation celebrated the inclusion of many ‘exotic’ species in Ruysch's paintings, it contained no discussion of how these specimens came to be in Western Europe. One wonders whether the exclusion in Munich and inclusion in the United States was a response to the needs and requests of local audiences, lenders and museum stakeholders. A disappointment in this otherwise superb exhibition was the overall lack of attention given to the exploration of the role of women in the illustration of nature (touched upon in Toledo only) and to the important contribution of women to the arts in the seventeenth century generally. The section of the exhibition focused on Anna and Rachel Ruysch, for example, likely left visitors with two impressions: first, that Anna was a talented copyist of Rachel's works but lacked the talent and ingenio of her sister when it came to succeeding in what was otherwise a man's world; and second, that like most women artists, Anna ceased painting when she married. Set against Anna, Rachel becomes an exception, a perception that has been increasingly undermined in recent exhibitions featuring female artists and makers. Unfortunately, the result is that viewers are not invited to imagine the many different ways in which women artists likely continued contributing to the arts after marriage. The accompanying catalogue, like the exhibition, is beautifully produced. Edited by Schindler, Ebert and Knapp, the volume is lavishly illustrated, filled with full-sized images of entire paintings as well as details. The volume contains the most up-to-date scholarship on Ruysch, an artist whose last monographic study in English (apart from Berardi's dissertation in 1998) was Maurice Grant's 1956 book, consisting of a two-page biography of the artist and a catalogue. The ten scholarly essays of the catalogue set out the latest research findings on Ruysch as well as important contextual information and directly support each of the four thematic pillars of the exhibition. Essays that stand out include Schindler's ‘Rachel Ruysch: A (Re)introduction’, in which the author frames the four themes of the exhibition. Schindler's thorough familiarity with the oeuvre of Ruysch shines through as he points to individual details in paintings to frame his narrative. The essay is exemplary in its willingness to take educated risks, notably in exploring the relationship between Ruysch and her sister Anna. Upon close inspection, Schindler suggests that the painting Flowers in a Vase (Figure 4) may have been a collaboration between the two sisters. This hypothesis is based on stylistic analysis as well as on the practical realities facing Ruysch: her works were highly popular, and it is not unlikely that she may have turned to her talented sister to assist in meeting demand. Although this attribution has not (yet) been accepted, Schindler's argument is convincing and worth exploring further not only with respect to this painting, but in taking a renewed approach to tracing the contributions of women artists in early modernity. Davis's ‘Painting the Botanical World’ is, as far as I am aware, the first to systematically consider the origin of specimens depicted in the oeuvre of a single artist. Identifying specimens and tracing their appearance in Ruysch's canvases overtime, Davis charts Ruysch's fascination with non-native species over the arc of her long career. A visual dissection of the Nelson-Atkins painting (Figure 2), juxtaposed with a world map of species' origins, makes it clear that Ruysch was an international artist in more ways than one. The essay ‘The Diversity and Beauty of Nature’, by Katharina Schmidt-Loske, functions as a pendant to Davis's essay, offering an overview of the diversity of insect life in Ruysch's paintings, based on a survey of eighty-nine of the artist's works (out of more than 250). As with flower and plant specimens, Ruysch's insects came from the four corners of the world. Knapp's essay ‘Amsterdam's Flora: Rachel Ruysch within a Network of Horticultural Collectors’, provides the context for both Davis's and Schmidt-Loske's essays. The Flora in the essay's title refers to Agnes Block, a Dutch botanist and art patron who was an important source of knowledge, material, and commissions for a wide network of artists, garden enthusiasts, and botanists alike. Although it contains a small number of unfortunate inaccurate assumptions (e.g., that Block built her country estate, Vijverhof, to display her wealth, 74) and factual errors (the portrait of Block and her family is by Jan Weenix, and not Jan Baptist Weenix, 76), the essay compellingly makes the case for the importance of the networks active in and around Amsterdam that made possible the possession and cultivation of the rare and uncommon specimens of flora and fauna identified in Ruysch's oeuvre. Rounding out the catalogue are essays by Bert van de Roemer (‘Art is Human Added to Nature’), which explore the relationship between art and nature in early modernity, Ebert (‘Beyond Beauty: Collecting Ruysch in the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries’), which explores the patronage of Ruysch, which was both high-ranking and international and Lieke van Deinsen (‘Painting with Poetry’), which discusses an anthology of poetry dedicated to Ruysch and her art, Dichterlovers voor de uitmuntende schilderesse mejuffrouwe Rache Ruisch. A technical analysis of the painting Collector Josephus Augustinus Brentano in his Picture Gallery, by Adriaan de Lelie (1813, Rijksmuseum, on loan from Stichting Brentano's Steun des Ouderdoms), discussed in the essay ‘Forever in Bloom’, by Josephina de Fouw, Nouchka de Keyser and Jorinde Koenen, supports the argument that Ruysch's works were prestigious to collect and display well into the nineteenth century. Taken together, these essays highlight not only the significance of Ruysch as an artist in her lifetime and thereafter but also in a context in which the examination and understanding of nature and its relationship to art and humans was of foremost importance. Glancing across galleries painted in tones of green and shades of mauve and pink ranging from pale lilac to dark peony, Ruysch's heavy cabbage roses and bright red opium poppies beckon, enveloping visitors in a luxurious atmosphere one can almost (or, in Toledo, actually) smell. Ruysch was one of the best-known artists of the Baroque in her time; the exquisiteness of her flower still lifes was acknowledged from the moment she first started painting them, in the early 1680s. In recent years, her paintings have been included in group exhibitions on women, still lifes and nature, and early modern Netherlandish art. However unlikely it may seem, Rachel Ruysch: Nature Into Art is the first significant monographic exhibition devoted to the artist in more than 300 years. The exhibition opened at the Alta Pinakothek Munich on 26 November 2024, from where it travelled to the Toledo Museum of Art, in Ohio (April to July 2025) and to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (August to December 2025). The catalogue that accompanies the exhibition contains the only comprehensive scholarly research on the artist since Marianne Berardi's 1998 unpublished (although publicly available) doctoral dissertation, from which the exhibition derives its title. This review concerns the exhibition at all three venues and the catalogue, published by MFA Publications.1 The exhibition is timely. The urgency of environmental devastation and climate concerns have prompted several major museums to present exhibitions on flora and fauna and the art of nature. Decades of insistence on better gender representation have jolted museums into prioritizing exhibitions featuring women artists.2 Nature Into Art meets the moment. It distinguishes itself from the other recent excellent exhibitions by bringing together a broad range of perspectives, as set out below. Curated by Bernd Ebert (AP), Robert Schindler (TMA) and Anna C. Knaap (MFA), the exhibition rests on a curatorial scaffolding of four thematic pillars (the names of which vary slightly across venues): An Auspicious Beginning, which explores Ruysch's evolution as a young artist; The Two Sisters, which features a visual conversation between Rachel and her younger sister, Anna, who was also a talented artist; Art, Nature, and Science, which sets the pursuit of the knowledge of flora and fauna and the embrace of empiricism as a contextual backdrop for the world in which Ruysch's art came into being; and Fame and Fortune, which consists of an overview of Ruysch's high-ranking patrons and of her success as one of the best-selling artists of her time. A core group of approximately thirty-five paintings by Ruysch traveled to each location, with others appearing at some of the venues only. A portrait of Ruysch at work by Michiel van Musscher in collaboration with Ruysch, introducing her as a confident artist, featured proudly at all three venues (Figure 1), on display for the first time since its acquisition by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Yet, the three iterations of the exhibition varied considerably from each other, not only in size (with the AP edition being the largest and the MFA's the smallest), with respect to the selection of works on display, with different approaches to exhibition design, but also in terms of focus. In Munich, Ebert placed the emphasis on the Elector Palatine's patronage of Ruysch, a decision which enabled the museum to highlight the strengths of German collections and the artist's connections to the country, which go back at least as far as 1708, when the Elector Palatine Johann Wilhelm, high-ranking in the Holy Roman Empire and son-in-law of Cosimo III de’ Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, named Ruysch court painter. Set against burgundy walls, paintings including Bouquet of Flowers from 1708 (Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen München), with its vibrant green praying mantis, invite close inspection. A portrait of Ruysch with her husband Juriaen Pool and their son Jan Willem (named in honour of the Elector), believed to be a collaboration by Ruysch and Pool, anchors this section and underscores the significance of the patronage for the artist. Particularly compelling is a case containing a large medallion of Johann Wilhelm, like the one his namesake wears around his neck in the family portrait, and a letter from Ruysch dated 1715, in which she described a painting intended for the Elector as filled with ‘strange and rare flowers’. These objects complement the paintings and are helpful in conveying the deep appreciation the Elector had for Ruysch—and vice versa. In contrast, the intersection of art and science was key to understanding Ruysch's work at the MFA. Occupying three galleries out of the exhibition's five, arrangements of mounted insects recalling colourful mosaics, dried plant specimens, cases with oversized books and works on paper intermingled with paintings to produce a dynamic display. As the eye travelled from specimens to illustrations, one could not help trying to locate the various insects and flowers in the paintings—a Baroque version of Where's Waldo with a Hercules beetle. The first gallery drew attention to the significance of Ruysch's upbringing, together with her sister Anna, in the world of wonder created by their father, the celebrated anatomist Frederik Ruysch. The second gallery foregrounded the network of botanical and entomological artists active in Amsterdam at the same time as Ruysch, including Maria Sibylla Merian, Alida Withoos and Herman Henstenburg. Although she almost certainly would have known at least some of these artists, this is a leap that is not made explicitly in the gallery nor in the catalogue. The third gallery, also the largest, was conceived as the centrepiece of the exhibition, with its display of Ruysch's illustrations of plants non-native to Western Europe. Based on the work of Charles C. Davis (professor of biology at Harvard University and curator of the Harvard University Herbaria), a map and a video convey the wide reach of the regents and caretakers of the Amsterdam botanical garden (then known as the hortus medicus) in obtaining specimens from Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Consequently, the focus of the MFA's installation was in sharp distinction to the approach at the AP, which situated Frederik Ruysch and the evolution of early modern natural history in a gallery that stood physically separated from the others, which arguably undermined the role of science in Ruysch's artistic practice. Unintentionally, however, Boston's attention to art and science had the converse effect of shifting the visitor's attention away from Ruysch as an artist of extraordinary talent. With fewer paintings on display than in Munich but more than in Boston, the exhibition design in Toledo featured a gallery layout that naturally guided the visitor through a narrative that began with Ruysch's early paintings, not unlike at the AP, set in conversation with those who influenced her, directly and indirectly, including her teacher Willem van Aelst and (near-) contemporaries such as Otto Marseus van Schrieck, Jan Davidsz. De Heem and Maria van Oosterwijck. In a competition that pits the young Ruysch against her mentors and predecessors—searching for the most realistic morning glory, the liveliest poppy, the most dynamic ornamental grass—it seems obvious that Ruysch is destined to surpass them all. As at the AP and the MFA, visitors to the TMA were treated to drawings by Ruysch's contemporaries, wet and dry specimens, as well as large, illustrated books. It was only here, however, that extra emphasis was given to the Surinam toad, which carries and hatches its eggs on its back. The toad was a rarity at the end of the seventeenth century in Amsterdam, engaging the study and fascination of experts and curieux alike, from Frederik Ruysch and polymath Nicolaas Witsen, among others. Toledo was the only location to display a drawing of the Surinam toad by Ruysch, which Schindler discovered in the archives of the Royal Society in London. Schindler's find is significant in a number of ways. The drawing, dating to c. 1688, is the only one securely attributed to Ruysch and one of the earliest representations of the toad in Western Europe, pre-dating Maria Sibylla Merian's by at least twelve years. It is a near-perfect match for a painting of the Surinam toad by Ruysch dated 1690 (Musée du Grand Siècle, Saint-Cloud), confirming that Ruysch relied on drawings in creating the compositions of at least some of her paintings, a practice that is not surprising but for which no evidence had previously been located. Furthermore, the presence of the drawing in the archives of the Royal Society, where it most likely accompanied a letter to the Society sent by Witsen, who was a member, offers further support for the participation of Ruysch in the networks connecting empirical science and natural history in late seventeenth-century Amsterdam. Emerging from a close encounter with the Surinam toad, a visitor then walked into the world of the elite patrons that supported Ruysch from an early time, the most significant of which, of course, was the Elector. As in Munich and Boston, the family portrait of Ruysch with Pool and their son took pride of place. Here, the chronological approach worked particularly well, as the period of time spanning the patronage of the Elector (who passed away in 1716, before Ruysch's last painting for him could be delivered) coincided with the peak of Ruysch's experimentation with complex compositions that included a wide number of species non-native to Western Europe (as noted by Davis in his catalogue essay), thereby linking the galleries intellectually as well as physically. At all three venues, the exhibition closed with the small paintings that Ruysch produced in her old age. These canvases, unlike the almost bombastic compositions such as the Nelson-Atkins Museum painting (see Figure 2), are subdued, in a softer colour palette. They feature simple compositions of local flowers. Dating from the 1730s and 1740s, these paintings reflect the aesthetic tendencies of the rococo. Importantly, they display the sensibilities of an artist who is proudly able to carry on doing what she loves—as the paintings Ruysch inscribed with her age attest. The intimate scale of these works creates a quiet bond between artist and viewer, a sentiment which is also evoked by a small portrait of Ruysch in ink by Aert Schouman dated 1749, one year before her death. Unlike the portrait by Van Musscher (Figure 1), the artist shown here is old, with sunken, wrinkled cheeks (Figure 3). The attributes that accompany the depiction of the artist include brushes, grapes and peaches, and the medallion of Johann Wilhelm—a reminder, if one was needed, that Ruysch remained an acclaimed artist to the end. The most engaging and innovative aspect of the exhibition across all venues was the exploration of the fluid relationship between art, nature and science, a topic that has received increasing scholarly attention over the past decade. Bringing this field of inquiry to the public is important; as Eric Jorink and Bart Ramakers (2011) noted, ‘in the early modern era the contemporary Latin terms ars and scientia were complementary rather than opposites, covering a spectrum of meanings such as skill, experience and knowledge’ such that ‘the meanings of the words are often interchangeable’. Interestingly, and perhaps surprisingly, the topics of imperial botany (which some scholars have termed biopiracy) and colonization were only directly addressed at the MFA and the TMA, the latter unfortunately in an area situated at the exit of the exhibition, which disconnected these practices from the beautiful art that they made possible. Although the AP installation celebrated the inclusion of many ‘exotic’ species in Ruysch's paintings, it contained no discussion of how these specimens came to be in Western Europe. One wonders whether the exclusion in Munich and inclusion in the United States was a response to the needs and requests of local audiences, lenders and museum stakeholders. A disappointment in this otherwise superb exhibition was the overall lack of attention given to the exploration of the role of women in the illustration of nature (touched upon in Toledo only) and to the important contribution of women to the arts in the seventeenth century generally. The section of the exhibition focused on Anna and Rachel Ruysch, for example, likely left visitors with two impressions: first, that Anna was a talented copyist of Rachel's works but lacked the talent and ingenio of her sister when it came to succeeding in what was otherwise a man's world; and second, that like most women artists, Anna ceased painting when she married. Set against Anna, Rachel becomes an exception, a perception that has been increasingly undermined in recent exhibitions featuring female artists and makers. Unfortunately, the result is that viewers are not invited to imagine the many different ways in which women artists likely continued contributing to the arts after marriage. The accompanying catalogue, like the exhibition, is beautifully produced. Edited by Schindler, Ebert and Knapp, the volume is lavishly illustrated, filled with full-sized images of entire paintings as well as details. The volume contains the most up-to-date scholarship on Ruysch, an artist whose last monographic study in English (apart from Berardi's dissertation in 1998) was Maurice Grant's 1956 book, consisting of a two-page biography of the artist and a catalogue. The ten scholarly essays of the catalogue set out the latest research findings on Ruysch as well as important contextual information and directly support each of the four thematic pillars of the exhibition. Essays that stand out include Schindler's ‘Rachel Ruysch: A (Re)introduction’, in which the author frames the four themes of the exhibition. Schindler's thorough familiarity with the oeuvre of Ruysch shines through as he points to individual details in paintings to frame his narrative. The essay is exemplary in its willingness to take educated risks, notably in exploring the relationship between Ruysch and her sister Anna. Upon close inspection, Schindler suggests that the painting Flowers in a Vase (Figure 4) may have been a collaboration between the two sisters. This hypothesis is based on stylistic analysis as well as on the practical realities facing Ruysch: her works were highly popular, and it is not unlikely that she may have turned to her talented sister to assist in meeting demand. Although this attribution has not (yet) been accepted, Schindler's argument is convincing and worth exploring further not only with respect to this painting, but in taking a renewed approach to tracing the contributions of women artists in early modernity. Davis's ‘Painting the Botanical World’ is, as far as I am aware, the first to systematically consider the origin of specimens depicted in the oeuvre of a single artist. Identifying specimens and tracing their appearance in Ruysch's canvases overtime, Davis charts Ruysch's fascination with non-native species over the arc of her long career. A visual dissection of the Nelson-Atkins painting (Figure 2), juxtaposed with a world map of species' origins, makes it clear that Ruysch was an international artist in more ways than one. The essay ‘The Diversity and Beauty of Nature’, by Katharina Schmidt-Loske, functions as a pendant to Davis's essay, offering an overview of the diversity of insect life in Ruysch's paintings, based on a survey of eighty-nine of the artist's works (out of more than 250). As with flower and plant specimens, Ruysch's insects came from the four corners of the world. Knapp's essay ‘Amsterdam's Flora: Rachel Ruysch within a Network of Horticultural Collectors’, provides the context for both Davis's and Schmidt-Loske's essays. The Flora in the essay's title refers to Agnes Block, a Dutch botanist and art patron who was an important source of knowledge, material, and commissions for a wide network of artists, garden enthusiasts, and botanists alike. Although it contains a small number of unfortunate inaccurate assumptions (e.g., that Block built her country estate, Vijverhof, to display her wealth, 74) and factual errors (the portrait of Block and her family is by Jan Weenix, and not Jan Baptist Weenix, 76), the essay compellingly makes the case for the importance of the networks active in and around Amsterdam that made possible the possession and cultivation of the rare and uncommon specimens of flora and fauna identified in Ruysch's oeuvre. Rounding out the catalogue are essays by Bert van de Roemer (‘Art is Human Added to Nature’), which explore the relationship between art and nature in early modernity, Ebert (‘Beyond Beauty: Collecting Ruysch in the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries’), which explores the patronage of Ruysch, which was both high-ranking and international and Lieke van Deinsen (‘Painting with Poetry’), which discusses an anthology of poetry dedicated to Ruysch and her art, Dichterlovers voor de uitmuntende schilderesse mejuffrouwe Rache Ruisch. A technical analysis of the painting Collector Josephus Augustinus Brentano in his Picture Gallery, by Adriaan de Lelie (1813, Rijksmuseum, on loan from Stichting Brentano's Steun des Ouderdoms), discussed in the essay ‘Forever in Bloom’, by Josephina de Fouw, Nouchka de Keyser and Jorinde Koenen, supports the argument that Ruysch's works were prestigious to collect and display well into the nineteenth century. Taken together, these essays highlight not only the significance of Ruysch as an artist in her lifetime and thereafter but also in a context in which the examination and understanding of nature and its relationship to art and humans was of foremost importance. title: Interactive analysis of urban heat island effect based on multisource data fusion and 3D geo-visualization
abstract: A transformer-based deep learning framework is developed for the interactive analysis of urban heat island (UHI) effects by fusing heterogeneous data sources—including advanced optical technologies such as multispectral imaging, optical imaging, and optical sensing—and enabling Three-Dimensional (3D) geo-visualization. The method integrates multispectral satellite imagery and optical sensor data with nighttime light data and 3D urban morphology through modality-specific encoders and a cross-modal alignment module, producing a unified latent representation of urban thermal environments. The spatial-temporal attention mechanism allows accurate prediction of localized risk of UHI impacts by modeling complex dependencies in the planar, vertical and temporal dimensions. A gradient-based attribution module quantifies the contribution of each urban feature and supports causality analysis and interpretability. The system's geo-visual interface identifies design parameter sensitivities and generates probabilistic risk maps. It can also generate dynamic isotherms. Extensive validation in the Guangzhou-Foshan metropolitan area demonstrates that the proposed methodology provides significant improvements in accuracy and generalization compared with conventional models, and successfully identifies key morphological drivers and microscale thermal anomalies. This study provides a powerful computational paradigm for scenario-driven urban form optimization, real-time assessment of urban risk, and high-resolution UHI modeling.
venue: Second International Conference on Communication, Information, and Digital Technologies (CIDT 2025)

title: Source framing triggers systematic bias in large language models.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate text, raising urgent questions about whether their judgments are consistent, unbiased, and robust to framing effects. Here, we examine inter- and intramodel agreement across four state-of-the-art LLMs tasked with evaluating 4800 narrative statements on 24 different topics of social, political, and public health relevance, for a total of 192,000 assessments. We manipulate the disclosed source of each statement to assess how attribution to either another LLM or a human author of specified nationality affects evaluation outcomes. Different LLMs display a remarkably high degree of inter- and intramodel agreement across topics, but this alignment breaks down when source framing is introduced. Attributing statements to Chinese individuals systematically lowers agreement scores across all models and, in particular, for DeepSeek Reasoner. Our findings show that LLMs' own judgment of agreement with narrative statements exhibit systematic bias from framing effects, with substantial implications for the neutrality and fairness of LLM-mediated information systems.
venue: Science advances

title: Neural network for natural language processing to determine treatment urgency in an ophthalmology emergency department.
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">In an ophthalmology emergency department, determining treatment urgency is crucial for patient safety and the efficient use of resources. The aim of this study was to use artificial intelligence to develop a neural network and evaluate its accuracy in predicting treatment urgency.</AbstractText>

title: Can Attention Be Used to Explain EHR-Based Mortality Prediction Tasks: A Case Study on Hemorrhagic Stroke.
abstract: Stroke is a significant cause of mortality and morbidity, necessitating early predictive strategies to minimize risks. Traditional methods for evaluating patients, such as Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II, IV) and Simplified Acute Physiology Score III (SAPS III), have limited accuracy and interpretability. This paper proposes a novel approach: an interpretable, attention-based transformer model for early stroke mortality prediction. This model seeks to address the limitations of previous predictive models, providing both interpretability (providing clear, understandable explanations of the model) and fidelity (giving a truthful explanation of the model's dynamics from input to output). Furthermore, the study explores and compares fidelity and interpretability scores using Shapley values and attention-based scores to improve model explainability. The research objectives include designing an interpretable attention-based transformer model, evaluating its performance compared to existing models, and providing feature importance derived from the model.

title: Leveraging Machine Learning Models for Trustworthy Prediction of Diabetes
abstract: A significant and widespread health issue among people of all ages is diabetes. Incorporating machine learning (ML) algorithms in clinical care can assist in the early detection of diabetes and preventing patients from experiencing significant health issues caused by the impact of diabetes. Furthermore, the most recent Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques may enable end users to understand and trust AI decisions. This research proposes an approach to detect diabetes by leveraging ML algorithms. The detection of diabetes allows for prompt medication, dietary, and lifestyle modifications, which enhance blood sugar regulation and lower the risk of complications from diabetes. Building a reliable machine learning model is influenced by several factors, including anomalies, data quality, and model selection. This work emphasizes building a trustworthy model to predict diabetes by overcoming the issues of missing data, anomalies, and appropriate model selection, along with an understanding of the results obtained by the model.

title: Uncovering Trauma in Genocide Tribunals
abstract: This paper applies Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods to analyze the exposure to trauma experienced by witnesses in international criminal tribunals when testifying in court. One major contribution of this study is the creation of a substantially extended version of the Genocide Transcript Corpus (GTC) that includes 52,845 text segments of transcripts from three different genocide tribunals. Based on this data, we first examine the prevalence of trauma-related content in witness statements. Second, we are implementing a binary classification algorithm to automatically detect potentially traumatic content. Therefore, in a preparatory step, an Active Learning (AL) approach is applied to establish the ideal size for the training data set. Subsequently, this data is used to train a transformer model. In this case, the two models BERTbase and HateBERT are used for both steps, allowing for a comparison of a base-level model with a model that has already been pre-trained on data more relevant in the context of harmful vocabulary. In a third step, the study employs an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) model to gain a deeper understanding of the reasoning behind the model's classifications. Our results suggest that both BERTbase and HateBERT perform comparatively well on this classification task, with no model clearly outperforming the other. The classification outcomes further suggest that a reduced data set size can achieve equally high performance metrics and might be a preferable choice in certain use cases. The results can be used to establish more trauma-informed legal procedures in genocide-related tribunals, including the identification of potentially re-traumatizing examination approaches at an early stage.
venue: Proceedings of the Nineteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law

One major contribution of this study is the creation of a substantially extended version of the Genocide Transcript Corpus (GTC) that includes 52,845 text segments of transcripts from three different genocide tribunals. Based on this data, we first examine the prevalence of trauma-related content in witness statements. Second, we are implementing a binary classification algorithm to automatically detect potentially traumatic content. Therefore, in a preparatory step, an Active Learning (AL) approach is applied to establish the ideal size for the training data set. Subsequently, this data is used to train a transformer model. In this case, the two models BERTbase and HateBERT are used for both steps, allowing for a comparison of a base-level model with a model that has already been pre-trained on data more relevant in the context of harmful vocabulary. In a third step, the study employs an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) model to gain a deeper understanding of the reasoning behind the model's classifications. Our results suggest that both BERTbase and HateBERT perform comparatively well on this classification task, with no model clearly outperforming the other. The classification outcomes further suggest that a reduced data set size can achieve equally high performance metrics and might be a preferable choice in certain use cases. The results can be used to establish more trauma-informed legal procedures in genocide-related tribunals, including the identification of potentially re-traumatizing examination approaches at an early stage.
venue: Proceedings of the Nineteenth International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law

title: Silencing the Risk, Not the Whistle: A Semi-automated Text Sanitization Tool for Mitigating the Risk of Whistleblower Re-Identification
abstract: Whistleblowing is essential for ensuring transparency and accountability in both public and private sectors. However, (potential) whistleblowers often fear or face retaliation, even when reporting anonymously. The specific content of their disclosures and their distinct writing style may re-identify them as the source. Legal measures, such as the EU Whistleblower Directive, are limited in their scope and effectiveness. Therefore, computational methods to prevent re-identification are important complementary tools for encouraging whistleblowers to come forward. However, current text sanitization tools follow a one-size-fits-all approach and take an overly limited view of anonymity. They aim to mitigate identification risk by replacing typical high-risk words (such as person names and other labels of named entities) and combinations thereof with placeholders. Such an approach, however, is inadequate for the whistleblowing scenario since it neglects further re-identification potential in textual features, including the whistleblower’s writing style. Therefore, we propose, implement, and evaluate a novel classification and mitigation strategy for rewriting texts that involves the whistleblower in the assessment of the risk and utility. Our prototypical tool semi-automatically evaluates risk at the word/term level and applies risk-adapted anonymization techniques to produce a grammatically disjointed yet appropriately sanitized text. We then use a Large Language Model (LLM) that we fine-tuned for paraphrasing to render this text coherent and style-neutral. We evaluate our tool’s effectiveness using court cases from the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and excerpts from a real-world whistleblower testimony and measure the protection against authorship attribution attacks and utility loss statistically using the popular IMDb62 movie reviews dataset, which consists of 62 individuals. Our method can significantly reduce authorship attribution accuracy from 98.81% to 31.22%, while preserving up to 73.1% of the original content’s semantics, as measured by the established cosine similarity of sentence embeddings.

title: Using Large Language Models to Compare Explainable Models for Smart Home Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Recognizing daily activities with unobtrusive sensors in smart environments enables various healthcare applications. Monitoring how subjects perform activities at home and their changes over time can reveal early symptoms of health issues, such as cognitive decline. Most approaches in this field use deep learning models, which are often seen as black boxes mapping sensor data to activities. However, non-expert users like clinicians need to trust and understand these models' outputs. Thus, eXplainable AI (XAI) methods for Human Activity Recognition have emerged to provide intuitive natural language explanations from these models. Different XAI methods generate different explanations, and their effectiveness is typically evaluated through user surveys, that are often challenging in terms of costs and fairness. This paper proposes an automatic evaluation method using Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify, in a pool of candidates, the best XAI approach for non-expert users. Our preliminary results suggest that LLM evaluation aligns with user surveys.
venue: Companion of the 2024 on ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing

title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.
venue: Proceedings of the 5th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: TABCF: Counterfactual Explanations for Tabular Data Using a Transformer-Based VAE
abstract: In the field of Explainable AI (XAI), counterfactual (CF) explanations are one prominent method to interpret a black-box model by suggesting changes to the input that would alter a prediction. In real-world applications, the input is predominantly in tabular form and comprised of mixed data types and complex feature interdependencies. These unique data characteristics are difficult to model, and we empirically show that they lead to bias towards specific feature types when generating CFs. To overcome this issue, we introduce TABCF, a CF explanation method that leverages a transformer-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) tailored for modeling tabular data. Our approach uses transformers to learn a continuous latent space and a novel Gumbel-Softmax detokenizer that enables precise categorical reconstruction while preserving end-to-end differentiability. Extensive quantitative evaluation on five financial datasets demonstrates that TABCF does not exhibit bias toward specific feature types, and outperforms existing methods in producing effective CFs that align with common CF desiderata.
venue: Proceedings of the 5th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance

title: Mitigating Risks in Marketplace Semantic Search: A Dataset for Harmful and Sensitive Query Alignment
abstract: Semantic search engines have transformed user interaction with online marketplaces, creating a need for effective methods to moderate harmful and sensitive content.Existing approaches often struggle with ambiguous query intent, content classification challenges, and noisy data, making it difficult to ensure user safety while maintaining relevance in search results.To address these challenges, we introduce SHIELD, a synthetic dataset designed for classifying user queries into harmful, sensitive, and normal categories.SHIELD is generated using a large language model with a structured taxonomy, followed by automated filtering using a reward model to ensure data quality and relevance.To demonstrate SHIELD's utility, we evaluate three classification approaches: (1) BM25, a computationally efficient retrieval-based method; (2) a sentence transformer with FAISS, which improves classification by leveraging semantic embeddings; and (3) MoralBERT, a fine-tuned transformer model trained on SHIELD for direct query classification.We discuss the trade-offs among these methods in terms of accuracy, resource requirements, and explainability, highlighting their applicability in real-world semantic search systems.This work provides a foundation for developing AI-driven content moderation systems in semantic search, offering insights into the trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and explainability.The SHIELD dataset, pre-trained model, and generation details are publicly available to support future research and real-world deployment: https://github.com/flpspacek/SHIELD.Warning: This paper contains examples of language and content that some readers may find offensive.These examples are included solely to illustrate challenges in content moderation and to highlight the importance of ethical considerations in semantic search systems.
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization

title: Adaptive XAI: Advancing Intelligent Interfaces for Tailored AI Explanations (2nd Edition)
abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in daily decision-making processes, the need for effective communication between humans and AI systems grows more crucial. The Adaptive XAI (AXAI) workshop, now in its second edition, focuses on developing intelligent interfaces that can adaptively explain AI’s decision-making processes. Building on the success of our inaugural event at IUI 2024, this workshop continues to explore the intersection of Explainable AI and adaptive user interfaces, emphasizing the development of interfaces that dynamically adapt to create explanations that resonate with diverse users. title: On the Generalization and Adaptation Ability of Machine-Generated Text Detectors in Academic Writing
abstract: The rising popularity of large language models (LLMs) has raised concerns about potential abuse and harmful content. As a result, developing a highly generalizable and adaptable machine-generated text (MGT) detection system has become an urgent priority. Given that LLMs are most commonly misused in academic writing, this work investigates the generalization and adaptation capabilities of MGT detectors in three key aspects specific to academic writing: First, we construct MGT-Academic, a large-scale dataset comprising over 336M tokens and 749K samples. MGT-Academic focuses on academic writing, featuring human-written texts (HWTs) and MGTs across STEM, Humanities, and Social Sciences, paired with an extensible code framework for efficient benchmarking. Second, we benchmark the performance of various detectors for binary classification and text attribution tasks in both in-domain and cross-domain settings. This benchmark reveals the often-overlooked challenges of text attribution tasks. Third, we introduce a novel text attribution task in which models must adapt to new classes over time, with little or no access to prior training data, spanning both few-shot and many-shot scenarios. We implement a range of adaptation techniques to enhance performance across these settings. Our findings provide new insights into the generalization ability of MGT detectors and lay the foundation for building robust, adaptive detection systems. The code framework is available at https://github.com/Y-L-LIU/MGTBench-2.0.
venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2

abstract: Hate crimes, driven by biases against specific demographic groups, harm not only individuals but undermine the security, trust, and cohesion of entire communities.Accurately identifying such crimes remains a significant challenge due to under-reporting, limited training, and the complexity of determining bias motivations.In this paper, we analyze the results of a text classification model developed to improve the precision of hate crime statistics and identification in Sweden.Empirical results indicate the model outperforms traditional manual police classification of hate crimes, achieving higher precision across various crime types and regions.We further disaggregate performance to pinpoint persistent challenges and highlight categories where both human and machine decision-makers struggle.While the model focuses on statistical estimation rather than direct case-level decision-making, we discuss the broader implications of algorithmic transparency, accountability, and explainability.Ultimately, this research illustrates how transformer-based neural networks can responsibly bolster the detection and understanding of hate crimes, informing policies to better protect vulnerable communities.

title: Correctness is not Faithfulness in Retrieval Augmented Generation Attributions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed information retrieval through chat interfaces, but their hallucination tendencies pose significant risks. While Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with citations has emerged as a solution by allowing users to verify responses through source attribution, current evaluation approaches focus primarily on citation correctness - whether cited documents support the corresponding statements. This is insufficient and we introduce citation faithfulness - whether the model's reliance on cited documents is genuine rather than post-rationalized to fit pre-existing knowledge. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we introduce coherent notions of attribution and introduce the concept of citation faithfulness; (ii) we propose desiderata for citations beyond correctness and accuracy needed for trustworthy systems; and (iii) we emphasize evaluating citation faithfulness by studying post-rationalization. Through experimentation, we reveal prevalent post-rationalization issues, finding that up to 57% of citations lack faithfulness. This undermines reliable attribution and may result in misplaced trust, highlighting a critical gap in current LLM-based IR systems. We demonstrate why both citation correctness and faithfulness must be considered when deploying LLMs in IR applications, contributing to a broader discussion of building more reliable and transparent information access systems.

title: User Compliance and Awareness towards Persuasive XAI: Investigating the Rhetorical Layer of LLM-generated Explanations
abstract: In high-stakes decision-making, the acceptance of AI recommendations depends not only on system accuracy but also on how decisions are explained. While prior work on explainable AI has largely focused on transparency and interpretability, less attention has been paid to the persuasive dimension of explanations. To address this gap, we investigate how rhetorical strategies drawn from Cialdini’s persuasion theory, when embedded in natural language explanations generated by large language models (LLMs), influence user compliance and their ability to recognize persuasive intent. We conducted a controlled survey study with 129 participants in two application domains—finance and healthcare—where participants evaluated both a baseline and a persuasive explanation for an AI-generated decision across favorable and unfavorable outcomes. In a complementary task, participants rated ten short explanations on perceived persuasiveness and factual strength, enabling us to measure awareness of persuasive intent. Our results show that persuasive explanations significantly increased compliance in the healthcare scenario (p <.001), whereas baseline explanations were more effective in finance (p <.001), regardless of whether the AI decision was positive or negative. A notable proportion of participants rated explanations containing at least one of Cialdini’s persuasion techniques as highly persuasive, yet simultaneously judged them to be factually weaker. Importantly, we found no statistically significant evidence that participants’ ability to recognize persuasive intent influenced compliance. These findings highlight the dual role of persuasive explanations: they can enhance foster compliance in sensitive contexts such as healthcare but risk undermining trust in domains like finance. For HCI and IUI, our study underscores that explanations are not neutral vessels of information: their rhetorical form substantially shapes how users perceive and engage with AI-assisted decision-making. Designers of explainable AI systems should therefore carefully balance transparency and persuasion when developing interfaces for high-stakes applications.

title: "Walk a Mile in My Voice": Voice Conversion Shapes Trust, Attribution, and Empathy in Human-AI Speech Interactions
abstract: Speech Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs) represent a new generation of conversational AI that processes spoken language directly from audio. This enables sensitivity to prosodic cues while also inheriting voice-based demographic information that has been shown to lead to biased system behaviour. Studying how people react and reflect on AI responses to different gender and accent presentation can contribute to understanding the potential societal impact. In this study, we examine how vocal identity factors of accent and perceived gender shape user evaluations of AI responses while the underlying linguistic content remains constant. Through two complementary studies (Interactive Study, N=24; Observational Study, N=19), we investigate whether experiencing interactions through voice converted identities versus observing pre-recorded conversations affects perceived harm, acceptability, trust, and responsibility attribution. We find that participants who experienced voice conversion rated benign AI responses as significantly more acceptable and reported significantly higher trust compared to those observing identical interactions, while perceived harm remained low across conditions. Qualitative feedback reveals that participants attributed different AI behaviours to voice characteristics, noting perceived differences in tone, helpfulness, and respect based on accent and gender presentation. Our findings suggest that vocal identity functions as a design variable, with systematic effects on user perception even when lexical content is held constant.

title: Meta-Learning Enhanced Explainability of Large Language Models for Low-Sample Transaction Monitoring in AML Compliance
abstract: In the atmosphere of the strict regulation of finance industry, AML compliance imposes higher demands on interpretability and identification attention of transaction monitoring systems under low-sample scenario, while the current rule-based systems have the limitation of data shortage and diversiform behavior patterns. Towards this end, in this work we introduce a novel and interpretable large language model framework Meta-XAML, enhanced by meta-learning, for more intelligent and transparent AML transaction monitoring in low-shot setting. On the one hand, the task adaptive meta-learner is capable of dynamically adapting the model parameters to the heterogeneity of customer behavior and trans-jurisdictional differences. Secondly, the attribution-guided interpretation module makes attention aligned with the causal mask mechanism of Shapley value, to achieve legally traceable interpretation for high-risk transactions. Furthermore, the model also formulates the objective of prototype constraint contrast learning for better semantic alignment and more robust expression under few shots. By jointly optimizing multiple objectives loss functions, the entire model is forced to be optimized to ensure: the classification accuracy, interpretation credibility, and cross-domain generalization ability. Experiments on the AML trading dataset demonstrate that Meta-XAML achieves 8.6% F1-score gain over the state-of-the-art competitors.
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Digital Finance

abstract: <jats:p>We propose a framework for evaluating carbon attribution methods for multi-tenant LLM serving. The framework formalizes the problem using three key components: (1) a set of requests with varying prompt and decode lengths, (2) the LLM inference runtime including batching algorithms, and (3) a carbon emission model accounting for both operational carbon (proportional to power consumption and carbon intensity) and embodied carbon from hardware manufacturing. title: A New Attack Surface: XAI-guided Adversarial Comment Generation with LLMs to Attack Fake News Detectors
abstract: The swift proliferation of false information on social media presents significant risks to public confidence and the stability of democracy, which motivates the development of machine learning and deep learning-based fake news detectors. While these systems can effectively analyze news content and user interactions, they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Prior research has focused mainly on modifying article text or retrieving generic user comments, leaving comment-based attack strategies underexplored. Existing comment-based attacks often rely on generating synthetic text that can be unrealistic or retrieving existing comments without strategic guidance that ignores feature importance. In this work, we introduce a novel attack surface that combines model interpretability with generative language models. Our approach uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to identify influential tokens driving fake or real classifications and prompts a large language model (LLM) to generate contextually credible human-like comments that utilize influential tokens. The generated comments are then appended to the article, evaluated against multiple state?of?the?art detectors (dEFEND, TextCNN, and RoBERTa), and compared against existing comment-based attacks such as MALCOM, CopyCat, and retrieval?based methods. Our XAI-guided LLM-based approach is competitive compared to existing generative and retrieval-based attack methods, with higher attack success rates while maintaining naturalness and contextual relevance.

While these systems can effectively analyze news content and user interactions, they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Prior research has focused mainly on modifying article text or retrieving generic user comments, leaving comment-based attack strategies underexplored. Existing comment-based attacks often rely on generating synthetic text that can be unrealistic or retrieving existing comments without strategic guidance that ignores feature importance. In this work, we introduce a novel attack surface that combines model interpretability with generative language models. Our approach uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to identify influential tokens driving fake or real classifications and prompts a large language model (LLM) to generate contextually credible human-like comments that utilize influential tokens. The generated comments are then appended to the article, evaluated against multiple state?of?the?art detectors (dEFEND, TextCNN, and RoBERTa), and compared against existing comment-based attacks such as MALCOM, CopyCat, and retrieval?based methods. Our XAI-guided LLM-based approach is competitive compared to existing generative and retrieval-based attack methods, with higher attack success rates while maintaining naturalness and contextual relevance.

title: Explainable and Efficient Hateful Meme Detection using Multimodal Vision-Language Fusion
abstract: Hateful memes combine images and text to express harmful meaning that often relies on subtle cross-modal cues. Detecting such content requires understanding both modalities and their interactions. Large vision–language models achieve strong accuracy but are typically opaque, slow, and impractical for deployment on moderate hardware. We introduce a lightweight and interpretable multimodal framework integrating a MobileNet-based visual encoder with a DistilBERT-based text encoder, fused through either simple concatenation or a compact cross-attention layer. The model achieves 0.80 ROC-AUC and 73% accuracy on the Facebook Hateful Memes benchmark, while producing Grad-CAM and token-level attribution explanations that clarify its predictions. Running efficiently on CPU, it shows that interpretable multimodal moderation is achievable without relying on large transformer architectures.

title: An Explainable AI Framework for Parkinson's Disease Prediction Using XGBoost, SHAP, and Large Language Model Integration
abstract: Parkinson’s disease is the fastest growing neurodegenerative disease worldwide currently. According to American Parkinson’s Disease Association, more than 10 million people are affected from this disease in different regions globally. This number is expected to increase to around 20 million in the coming decade. Risk management through early prediction can improve these outcomes but the clinical dependency now largely focuses on subjective examination which often delay the treatment and thereby worsens the condition of the patient. These current methods lack both explainability and interpretability, which is very important in neurodegenerative diseases. Our proposed method introduces a comprehensive framework that is created by integrating high performing machine learning algorithm with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and large language model (LLM). It targets to produce predictive accuracy and explainability. This entire system is easily understandable through user interface to the clinical users and patients. Our proposed method started with data preprocessing. After that we extracted the features using systematic evaluation of multiple classifiers. The test results showed that the XGBoost method outperformed other models in terms of accuracy, F1-score, precision, recall, and AUC. But only this prediction scores lacked explainability. To remove this limitations of traditional machine learning algorithms we applied SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to determine the feature-wise contribution of model predictions that how much influence a feature does have in occurring an individual patient’s parkinson disease. It is patient specific and transparent. It demonstrates the reason of Parkinson’s disease feature wise. Furthermore, we extended this explainability by integrating it with Meta-LLaMa-3 that transforms the SHAP results into natural language clinical explanation through an user interface. It shows the predictive reasons of the Parkinson’s disease and confidence score of having the risk of the disease to the physicians and the patient as a outcome.
venue: Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Next Generation Computing, Communication, Systems and Security

title: FedNova-Adaptive-based Cross-Jurisdictional Anti-Money Laundering Federated Diagnostic Framework
abstract: Difficulty implementing centralized anti-money laundering (AML) compliance diagnostics is exacerbated by fragmented cross-jurisdictional regulation, data silos, and privacy restrictions. Both NLP and big data analytics enable technical feasibility for rapid cross-border identification of potential compliance problems and legal risk. This paper presents the FedNova-Adaptive cross-jurisdiction AML federated diagnostic framework (FedNovaAML), at the semantic layer, multi-language legal NLP (SAR/KYC/policies) with rule prompts, align red flags across jurisdictions; at the risk layer, the temporal heterogeneous graph encodes the ‘entity-transaction-device-jurisdiction’ relationships and includes sanctions/PEP priors; at the federated layer, adaptive normalization on FedNova (for label bias, gradients variance, and time-lag reweighting) augmented with multi-task heads along with IRM alignment, meta-learning personalization, and sparse error feedback communication. We also describe measures for strong privacy and compliance via secure aggregation, DP-SGD, and split learning; not forgetting to mention how the temporal heterogeneous graph GNN achieves uncertainty calibration and that we use SHAP for post-hoc additive feature attribution to support auditability, while counterfactual explanations are treated as a separate class of explanations to suggest actionable changes. Our experiment demonstrates that our framework improves AUPRC by 7-15% and reduces false positive rates by 23% compared to the baseline.
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 International Symposium on Machine Learning and Social Computing

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Psychiatric disorders affect millions, yet diagnosis depends on subjective assessments and uneven access to care. To address these challenges, there is a growing need for Contestable AI (CAI), a framework that extends beyond Explainable AI (XAI) by allowing clinicians to inspect, question, and revise algorithmic outputs, thereby reducing automation bias and strengthening accountability. We present Heart2Mind
                    <jats:xref ref-type="fn">
                      <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                    </jats:xref>
                    , a human-centered CAI system for psychiatric disorder prediction that provides objective evidence while preserving clinical oversight. Heart2Mind collects R-R interval (RRI) time series from Polar H9/H10 wearable ECG sensors via a Cardiac Monitoring Interface and analyzes them using a Multi-Scale Temporal-Frequency Transformer (MSTFT) that combines time-domain and frequency-domain features. For contestability, the Contestable Diagnosis Interface integrates model explanations with dialogue. Self-Adversarial Explanations compare attention-based and gradient-based explanation maps to flag inconsistent predictions, and a collaboration chatbot helps users verify and challenge outputs. On the HRV-ACC dataset, MSTFT achieved 91.7% accuracy under leave-one-out cross-validation, outperforming benchmark methods. Human-centered evaluation with the Human-CAI Consensus Rate showed experts and CAI could confirm correct decisions and correct errors through readable, efficient dialogues (
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="LaTeX" version="MathJax">\(FKGL\approx 15\)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , median 8.3 minutes, 4 turns). These results support low-cost wearable CAI screening with objective biomarkers, safeguards, and an interactive path for clinicians to refine recommendations.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI in Automated and Remote UX Evaluation: A Systematic Review (2014–2024)
abstract: <jats:p>This systematic literature review examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into automated and remote usability and user experience (UX) evaluation methods. Synthesizing insights from 55 peer‐reviewed articles published between 2014 and 2024, the review identifies key AI technologies, such as machine learning, large language models (LLMs), generative AI (GenAI), and ChatGPT, and their roles in enhancing UX evaluation practices. While these technologies contribute to behavior modeling, sentiment analysis, feedback generation, and user simulation, their increasing use also introduces critical challenges. AI models often function as opaque “black boxes,” raising concerns about transparency, hallucinated outputs, contextual misinterpretation, and data bias. The review underscores the need for explainable, human‐in‐the‐loop AI systems, standardized evaluation frameworks, and responsible deployment practices. Specific implications for practice include integrating explainable AI (XAI) methods such as SHAP and counterfactual explanations to improve the transparency of UX insights; adopting domain adaptation and transfer learning to improve generalizability across platforms, demographics, and task contexts; and ensuring human oversight through human‐in‐the‐loop mechanisms to mitigate risks such as hallucinations and contextual misinterpretation. This study offers a comprehensive foundation for both future research and informed adoption of AI technologies in UX workflows, supporting more efficient, data‐driven, and human‐centered evaluation strategies.</jats:p>

title: Transparent precision: Explainable AI empowered breast cancer recommendations for personalized treatment
abstract: <jats:p><p>Breast cancer stands as a prevalent global concern, prompting extensive research into its origins and personalized treatment through Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven precision medicine. However, AI's black box nature hinders result acceptance. This study delves into Explainable AI (XAI) integration for breast cancer precision medicine recommendations. Transparent AI models, fuelled by patient data, enable personalized treatment recommendations. Techniques like feature analysis and decision trees enhance transparency, fostering trust between medical practitioners and patients. This harmonizes AI's potential with the imperative for clear medical decisions, propelling breast cancer care within the precision medicine era. This research work is dedicated to leveraging clinical and genomic data from samples of metastatic breast cancer. The primary aim is to develop a machine learning (ML) model capable of predicting optimal treatment approaches, including but not limited to hormonal therapy, chemotherapy, and anti-HER2 therapy. The objective is to enhance treatment selection by harnessing advanced computational techniques and comprehensive data analysis. A decision tree model developed here for the prediction of suitable personalized treatment for breast cancer patients achieves 99.87% overall prediction accuracy. Thus, the use of XAI in healthcare will build trust in doctors as well as patients.</p></jats:p>
venue: IAES International Journal of Artificial Intelligence (IJ-AI)
