title: Contextualized clinical anomaly detection with explainable AI and patient modeling
abstract: <jats:p><p>This study aims to reduce alarm fatigue and improve the clinical relevance of alerts in intensive care by combining sequential modeling, patient contextualization, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and probability calibration. To this end, we leverage the adult cohorts from MIMIC-III/IV, segmented into four-hour windows, explicitly handling missing data and constructing a context vector that integrates demographics, comorbidities, and therapeutic interventions. The approach relies on a tabular autoencoder, an long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder, and a transformer, complemented by an adjustment layer based on auditable clinical rules, local explanations (LIME/SHAP), and post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling). Evaluation involves receiver operating characteristic (ROC)/precision–recall (PR) area under the curve (AUC), F1-score, sensitivity and specificity, as well as calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score), alert burden, ablation studies, robustness tests, and subgroup fairness analyses. Across all experiments, the complete model (+Context+XAI+Calibration) outperforms baselines in AUPRC and F1, reduces alert burden, and improves calibration while providing understandable explanations. Specifically, the proposed model improves ROC AUC from 0.74 to 0.89 and reduces alert burden by approximately one third compared to clinical thresholds.</p></jats:p>

title: Contextualized clinical anomaly detection with explainable AI and patient modeling
abstract: <jats:p><p>This study aims to reduce alarm fatigue and improve the clinical relevance of alerts in intensive care by combining sequential modeling, patient contextualization, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and probability calibration. To this end, we leverage the adult cohorts from MIMIC-III/IV, segmented into four-hour windows, explicitly handling missing data and constructing a context vector that integrates demographics, comorbidities, and therapeutic interventions. The approach relies on a tabular autoencoder, an long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder, and a transformer, complemented by an adjustment layer based on auditable clinical rules, local explanations (LIME/SHAP), and post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling). Evaluation involves receiver operating characteristic (ROC)/precision–recall (PR) area under the curve (AUC), F1-score, sensitivity and specificity, as well as calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score), alert burden, ablation studies, robustness tests, and subgroup fairness analyses. Across all experiments, the complete model (+Context+XAI+Calibration) outperforms baselines in AUPRC and F1, reduces alert burden, and improves calibration while providing understandable explanations. Specifically, the proposed model improves ROC AUC from 0.74 to 0.89 and reduces alert burden by approximately one third compared to clinical thresholds.</p></jats:p>

title: Bright Circle: Five Remarkable Women in the Age of Transcendentalism. By Randall Fuller
abstract: In Bright Circle, Randall Fuller takes on the by now familiar, yet still welcome, work of centering women in literary and philosophical traditions from which they have been excluded. He chooses five women active within the friendship and family networks that constituted American Transcendentalism: Mary Moody Emerson, Elizabeth Palmer Peabody, Sophia Peabody Hawthorne, Lidian Jackson Emerson, and Margaret Fuller. His claims will be familiar to many within the study of American Transcendentalism, new to some. He emphasizes the centrality of women's intellectual, artistic, and domestic work to Transcendentalism, focusing on Margaret Fuller's Conversations, Elizabeth Peabody's bookshop, and writings by all five women. He argues that these women, while providing writers like Emerson and Thoreau with their foundational ideas, were the most averse to what he calls Transcendentalism's “wispy idealism” (329). Part of Fuller's project is to recenter Transcendentalism in Boston, and while many of us have long seen Transcendentalism as multi-centered in location as it was multi-dimensional in thought and expression, for others, Concord may still function as its singular center. Fuller's work offers a correction to that misprision. Also welcome is the still needed refocusing on women. Nearly 30 years ago, Phyllis Cole published her groundbreaking study of Mary Moody Emerson, considering that Emerson one of the hallmark American thinkers of the late 18th century, and as the title of her book tells us, one of the major players in the “origins of Transcendentalism.”The past 30 years have seen excellent attention to these originating and participating thinkers of and within Transcendentalism. In addition to Cole's Mary Moody Emerson and the Origins of Transcendentalism (1998), we have seen Joan Goodwin's The Remarkable Mrs. Ripley: The Life of Sarah Alden Bradford Ripley (1998); Megan Marshall's Pulitzer-nominated Peabody Sisters: Three Women Who Ignited American Romanticism (2005) as well as her Pulitzer Prize-winning biography Margaret Fuller: A New American Life (2013); Helen Deese's Daughter of Boston: The Extraordinary Diary of a Nineteenth-Century Woman, Caroline Healey Dall (2006), as well as her extensive work editing Dall's journals. The field has been rich in single-authored volumes as well as in multi-authored essay collections.In their incisive summation of the work done then to date (2014), Cole and Jana Argersinger describe the foundational work that began with the textual recovery projects of the 1970s and 1980s, many of which continue to this day. “For over thirty years,” they wrote, “a veritable scholarly industry has been widening the base for understanding transcendentalism, even as the women's studies movement has overturned the canon with its body of recovery work” (7). Their essay opens Toward a Female Genealogy of Transcendentalism, a volume that includes primary source material interwoven with essays focusing on 17 different women within the Transcendentalist world. It includes substantive discussions of women at Brook Farm and the African American women of the Women's Era Club. The book includes essays on four out of the five women Fuller chooses as his subjects, but surprisingly he seems to have missed out on most of the book, briefly mentioning it only in relation to Mary Moody Emerson.Fuller's book raises concerns far more complicated than a book review can encompass. What follows is only a beginning. In the spirit of Transcendentalism, it centers questions and provocations to thought. When Christopher Pearse Cranch or Lidian Jackson Emerson articulated their satirical takes on their friends’—and indeed loved ones’—work, they participated in the provocation long esteemed by communities of activist thinkers. When Caroline Sturgis described herself as an endless questioner, she spoke for many within the Transcendentalist friendship groups. To borrow a phrase from their intellectual predecessors that remains apt in ours, theirs were lives devoted to “free and frank inquiry.”Turning to questions that are especially pertinent within Transcendentalism but relevant to all fields of literary study: As scholars, how do we grapple with what our fields have neglected or outright dismissed? Especially now, nearly a half century into concerted and excellent recovery work, how do we increase accessibility to lesser-known writings, and how also do we address the failings in such works and in their authors? A crucial dimension of that question involves turning the mirror on ourselves, directly engaging with the work that has made ours possible and examining the problems that persist within our own interpretive frameworks. Most importantly, how do we continually ask ourselves who is missing from our studies? To put the matter bluntly, as did Eric Gardner in his essay for Cole and Argersinger, while American Transcendentalism may have seemed the “‘whitest’ of spaces,” that may reveal our own failure to see who actually was there.I wish I could say that Fuller's book provides us exemplary answers to these questions. But unfortunately, I often found myself confronting the many and varied pitfalls we face in our scholarship. Ironically, for a book that centers the collective nature of women's writings and their activist work, his own approach remains distinctly individualistic. One of his central tenets is that individualism fatally flawed Transcendentalism. He emphasizes how the (male) Transcendentalists’ focus on the abstract “Individual” obscured contributions made by real individuals. Bringing forward these five women's contributions, he spotlights each woman in turn, and yet his approach oddly obscures the work upon which his depends. In his chapter narratives, he rarely discusses previous scholars’ work, giving only broad and unspecified acknowledgment in the introduction (7). There are short bibliographic essays for each figure at the end of the book; some significant books and articles are absent from this section, including Leslie Perrin Wilson's “‘No Worthless Books’: Elizabeth Peabody's Foreign Library, 1840–1852.” Copious endnotes source quotations, often by page number or “as quoted in.”Yet neither in the endmatter nor in the body of his work does he attempt to situate his own interpretations within the much larger conversation of the past 50 years. For example, it is alarming in the chapter on Sophia Peabody to find no reference to Marshall's significant discussion of how Peabody's Cuba Journal anticipated Emerson's and Thoreau's writings about the natural world (Marshall 278; Fuller 129), nor mention of Patricia Dunleavy Valenti's discussion of Peabody's early statements of Transcendentalism in the same journal.1 Similarly, with Fuller's commentary on how Mary Moody Emerson articulated ideas that later appeared in Waldo Emerson's writing, there is no direct engagement with Cole's close and detailed discussions of the topic. Another surprising omission occurs in his chapter on Lidian Jackson Emerson. Fuller's discussion of the gathering in Concord shortly after the Phi Beta Kappa address seems beholden to Cole's excellent essay, “Men and Women Conversing: The Emersons in 1837” (in Emersonian Circles: Essays in Honor of Joel Myerson, Wesley T. Mott and Robert E. Burkholder, eds., 1997).It is disconcerting to see the groundbreaking interpretations made by others—interpretations that have been integral to redefining the field—presented without attribution. Have such interpretations succeeded so well that they have become “common knowledge,” repeated freely by all, no longer needing to credit the thinkers who originated them? This remains a troubling question, calling us to consider just what our responsibility as scholars is. How do we situate our ideas in relation to others’ work, continuing the conversation and inviting others to join? Especially given the fraught nature of most recovery and reinterpretation projects, direct and transparent engagement with earlier work always seems called for, especially in a book in which one of the central claims is how women thinkers received little to no credit for originating and first articulating key elements within Transcendentalism. While I understand Fuller's choice may have been driven by his desire to write a seamless biographical narrative for each figure, seams need not always be invisible.Recovery work entails interpretation or, as the case usually is, significant reinterpretation that upends previously held assumptions. Dismissal or neglect often turns on an era's own biases: what prejudices prevented scholars from recognizing the merits of a work? What have readers failed to see because their own interpretive strategies stood in the way? As Margaret Fuller aptly reminded herself and her readers, a work needs to be read on its own terms. Her comment is particularly generative when it comes to the experiments in genre undertaken by the Transcendentalists, whether in the variations within their poetry, philosophic dialogues, dream-like prose vignettes or the varieties of journal-keeping they undertook. Even Bronson Alcott's much maligned “Orphic Sayings” might yet open to a reader who generates an interpretive strategy appropriate to its form.While Fuller's project is primarily biographical, he does bring attention to varieties of literary innovation, most signally with Mary Moody Emerson's Almanacks. At the same time, in the spirit of encouraging further interest and acknowledging previous and ongoing projects, one wishes he had substantively mentioned the brilliant work done by Noelle Baker and Sandra Petrulionis in building ways to read Mary Moody Emerson's work as well as in making that work readily available to others.2 Their extensive and ongoing digital edition, designed to “think through issues of display, reading practice, [and] the representation of documentary materiality,” together with Baker's articles, have truly made it possible to read work that might remain impenetrable. Both to encourage further study and to acknowledge the work already accomplished, one could wish for more direct and detailed comment somewhere in the chapters themselves—whether in the chapter focused on Mary Moody Emerson or in the epilogue noting the fate of her manuscripts. It is unfortunate that Fuller relies on the earlier Tolman transcripts now considered a problematic source, given their inaccuracies.Not only may we need to develop new methods for reading unfamiliar genres, but also and always, as scholars, we need to question rigorously our own interpretive frameworks, to see how they are holding up. As Argersinger and Cole point out, older models of scholarship depended upon sharp contrasts that suited a methodology based in oppositional thinking. Either/or was the governing paradigm. Contrast was paramount, often to the point of mutual exclusivity. Cole and Argersinger observe, “At times these currents of scholarship apparently stood in opposition, discovering antagonistic 19th-century cultures. We hope to move beyond such a standoff” (7). That hope has not yet been realized. Fuller draws upon heightened contrasts to structure interpretations based in highly dramatic prose. This is most notable in his comments on Transcendentalist idealism and prominent in his frequent use of tropes associated with “romantic” love narratives. Such either/or framing steadily fuels dramatization but readily obscures complexity. The Transcendentalists’ discussions—whether the topic was love, marriage, genius, the self and its vexed nature, principled engagement in societal reform—were nothing if not multidimensional, overlapping, and deeply intertwined. While they can be framed within an either/or paradigm, such bifurcation occludes the richness of difference among their varying perspectives.Interpretive frameworks come with their own vocabularies. Unfortunately, within Transcendentalist studies, oppositional thinking traded heavily in gendered stereotypes. Present throughout the book are painful phrasings that replicate the very biases he seeks to overturn. Women are “garrulous,” “incessant” talkers (154, 348). With such phrases, a woman's ready and powerful verbal fluency is diminished into an irritating habit. Mary Moody Emerson's interest in and indeed deep concern about theological matters is described as “her endless barrage of theological questions” for a “tolerant minister” (37). For Margaret Fuller, “talk was her salvation,” as if her brilliant ability to speak extemporaneously could only be explained by neediness (246). Elizabeth Peabody comes across as a money-making schemer, or as someone who was admired “despite her meddlesomeness and abstraction and incessant torrent of talk” (348). Even as he emphasizes the fact that Peabody had to make money to support the many members of her family, he undercuts that emphasis with damaging, toss-away phrases.The cumulative effect of such language is distracting, not to mention dispiriting. Women are “smitten”; they fall “hopelessly” or “headlong” in love (75, 273, 298). Intellectual activity is described as something “aswirl inside” a woman (in this case, describing Elizabeth Peabody, 94). Lydia Jackson is attracted to Emerson, not so much for his thought-provoking ideas as for the sound of his voice. Might it not be both? In the Conversations, certain participants seem to lack agency over their own expression. In his dramatic recreations, for example, ideas “gush forth”; Sophia Ripley “suddenly burst[s] out with a new idea”; Margaret Fuller is “suddenly struck with a new thought” (269, 271, 281). Even as he seeks to emphasize his subjects’ intellectual power, he casually takes it away: Elizabeth Peabody has a “knack for knowing the latest trends in thought and culture” (emphasis added), rather than amplifying her incisive attention and expansive reading, not to mention facility with several languages (177). Margaret Fuller “lashes out” at Emerson when she is not charming him (277, 193).In each case, the verbs seem oddly matched to the evidence. For example, in the descriptions of Fuller (“lashed out,” “charmed”) such conclusions are not foregone given what was written at the time. Emerson notes in his journal: “S.M.F. writes me that she waits for the Lectures seeing well after much intercourse that the best of me is there. She says very truly.”3 Were her words an emotional outburst as R. Fuller renders them through his phrase “lashed out”? Was this less reactive, one of Fuller's characteristically frank assessments of her friends’ strengths and weaknesses? No record remains from Fuller herself to provide her words or her reflections on the intent behind them. In the matter of “charming” the Emersons, R. Fuller's description turns on Lidian's report to Elizabeth Peabody after Fuller's initial visit to Concord. She writes, “you will be glad to hear that we find real satisfaction—Miss F. Mr E. & myself—in our intercourse with each other.” She expresses surprise that everything went so well, given the fact that each person held strong convictions that could readily put them at odds: “We like her—she likes us—I speak in this way—because you know we came together almost strangers—all to one another and the result of the experiment . . .—was doubtful—the tendencies of all three being strong & decided—and possibly not such as could harmonize.”4 I find myself hard pressed to equate “satisfaction” and unexpected consonance with “charm.”For those who would argue that such matters of diction are insignificant in a book this size, consider the cumulative effect and influence. In his New Yorker essay prompted by the recently published Library of America edition of Margaret Fuller's writings, James Marcus notes that Margaret Fuller seems to be enjoying something of a moment. He mentions Allison Pataki's novel based on Fuller's life as well as Bright Circle. In his description, Marcus characterizes Margaret Fuller as an “incurable gossip,” an idea that arises less from Pataki's novel than from R. Fuller's discussion, in which we are told that the Conversations brought women together for “laughter and gossip,” and that Margaret Fuller “gossiped” to Elizabeth Hoar in a letter about meeting George Sand (193, 302). Indeed, R. title: Public sentiment-based stock selection strategy using the BERT model and LightGBM algorithm
abstract: <jats:p>This paper develops a novel approach to stock selection by integrating natural language processing techniques with machine learning algorithms to analyze public opinion data in financial markets. Specifically, we employ the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model to process and classify financial news and social media content, combined with the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) algorithm to select high-potential stocks within identified concept sectors. Using over 18 million Chinese financial text records from 2023 to 2024, we construct a comprehensive framework that captures both market sentiment and stock-specific characteristics. Our strategy consists of three core components: (1) a BERT-based sentiment analyzer that identifies promising concept sectors with strong momentum, (2) a LightGBM-powered stock selection mechanism utilizing a specially designed “Concept-Momentum-Combined” factor alongside conventional financial indicators, and (3) a risk management system combining sentiment anomaly detection with multi-stage Average True Range (ATR) trailing stop mechanisms. Empirical results demonstrate significant outperformance over CSI 800 across various timeframes, with annualized excess returns of 21.55% over a six-month period and maximum drawdowns of only 11.68%. Performance attribution analysis confirms that concept sector selection based on sentiment analysis is the primary driver of excess returns. Our results add to the expanding literature on the use of artificial intelligence in financial markets and provide actionable takeaways for investors who would like to incorporate public opinion data into their investment process.</jats:p>

title: ChatGPT as a clinical support tool: A comprehensive review of applications, assessment, and implementation challenges
abstract: <jats:p>This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 296 core Web of Science publications to evaluate ChatGPT’s utility across modern medicine through a three-tiered framework: (1) Data Management (e.g., automating medical information extraction, enhancing electronic health record (EHR) integration, and optimizing clinical documentation workflows), (2) Clinical Decision Support (demonstrating capability in diagnostic accuracy and effective treatment), and (3) Therapeutic Support & Patient Services (facilitating personalized patient education via multilingual interaction and accelerating drug discovery). Additionally, dialogue-based AI frameworks, which prioritize communication efficacy over diagnostic performance, show particular promise in physiotherapy contexts. While ChatGPT demonstrates potential in enhancing operational efficiency, diagnostic speed, and personalizing patient management, key challenges still persist: data inaccuracies (e.g., hallucinated references), algorithmic biases (e.g., gender or racial disparities in treatment suggestions), insufficient clinical validation (overreliance on pattern recognition without physiological causality), communication barriers (misinterpretation of nuanced symptoms), ethical risks (privacy breaches in unsecured deployments) and other related issues. Successful implementation requires prioritizing five critical research avenues: (1) enhancing multimodal data analysis with diverse, domain-specific training datasets; (2) advancing explainable AI (XAI) techniques to improve algorithmic transparency/ clinician trust; (3) conducting multi-specialty validation through randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing safety and cost-effectiveness in real-world settings; (4) establishing adaptive ethical frameworks balancing innovation with patient rights, fairness, and harm prevention; (5) optimizing Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) applications via syndrome differentiation for complex comorbidities.</jats:p>

title: A temporal deep learning algorithm for prediction of extubation failures in critical care patients
abstract: <bold>Background:</bold> Failure of extubation was related to poor outcomes in ICU patients. Existing prediciton models for extubation failure were missing the dynamic fluctuations of disease status in the critically ill. This study proposes the TrAcE model, a deep learning-based tool that integrates static and temporal data with explainable results to improve prediction accuracy for extubation failure. <bold>Methods:</bold> Data from MIMIC-III was used for model training and validation. And PKUPH-Ext (The Peking University People’s Hospital- Extubation) data set was used for model testing. The model was trained with a Temporal Fusion Transformer- based neural network. Model performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC) and area under the precision recall curve (AUPRC). To ensure model explainability, the Captum library’s occlusion method identified feature attributions at population and individual levels. The TrAcE model’s extubation timing was compared to the spontaneous breathing test (SBT) guided extubation in the PKUPH-Ext dataset. <bold>Findings:</bold> The TrAcE model outperformed other models, achieving AUROCs of 0.823 (95% CI: 0.808-0.838) in the validation set and 0.859 (95% CI: 0.836-0.881) in the test set. AUPRCs were similarly favorable (0.734 and 0.757, respectively). In comparison with the SBT in the PKUPH-Ext set, TrAcE demonstrated superior performance and identified suitable extubation days earlier than SBT (4.32[IQR 0-20] vs 5.65[IQR 0-23], p<0.01). <bold>Conclusion:</bold> In the present study, we developed a deep learning model for predicting extubation failure in critical care patients. This model provides risk prediction and explainability in real-time.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in medical imaging: a systematic review of techniques, applications, and challenges.
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is crucial for enhancing transparency and trustworthiness, as well as for developing AI-based diagnostic systems in medical imaging to achieve clinical acceptability and reliability. This synthesis aligns with the current context of XAI in medical imaging on four key dimensions: trends in techniques, their application to clinical use cases or with human subjects, and the associated problems. In radiology and pathology, we report on image analysis based on current literature from credible databases. This review extends on the existing surveys by explicitly addressing the focus on feature selection (FS), graph neural networks (GNNs), and multimodal transformers and combining them to a cohesive XAI taxonomy and matches the techniques to the specific impact points in the clinical workflow in radiology and pathology. We present saliency maps, attention mechanisms, and gradient-based and rule-based elucidations of deep learning (DL) models in today’s healthcare environment. Finally, the results show that XAI significantly enhances overall clinical decision-making by making the high-level reasoning of the model readily available to users, thereby increasing their confidence in clinical decisions despite the remaining obstacles, including standardization, interpretability, data bias, and complicated data integration. From 980 records, 289 duplicates were removed, 691 screened, 209 excluded, 482 full texts assessed, 263 excluded with 219 yielding 133 included studies. Exploring this third dimension within an XAI environment identifies research gaps and paves the way for robust medical imaging XAI solutions. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Towards proactive palliative care in oncology: developing an explainable EHR-based machine learning model for mortality risk prediction.
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Ex-ante identification of the last year in life facilitates a proactive palliative approach. Machine learning models trained on electronic health records (EHR) demonstrate promising performance in cancer prognostication. However, gaps in literature include incomplete reporting of model performance, inadequate alignment of model formulation with implementation use-case, and insufficient explainability hindering trust and adoption in clinical settings. Hence, we aim to develop an explainable machine learning EHR-based model that prompts palliative care processes by predicting for 365-day mortality risk among patients with advanced cancer within an outpatient setting.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">Our cohort consisted of 5,926 adults diagnosed with Stage 3 or 4 solid organ cancer between July 1, 2017, and June 30, 2020 and receiving ambulatory cancer care within a tertiary center. The classification problem was modelled using Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and aligned to our envisioned use-case: "Given a prediction point that corresponds to an outpatient cancer encounter, predict for mortality within 365-days from prediction point, using EHR data up to 365-days prior." The model was trained with 75% of the dataset (n = 39,416 outpatient encounters) and validated on a 25% hold-out dataset (n = 13,122 outpatient encounters). To explain model outputs, we used Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values. Clinical characteristics, laboratory tests and treatment data were used to train the model. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), while model calibration was assessed using the Brier score.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">In total, 17,149 of the 52,538 prediction points (32.6%) had a mortality event within the 365-day prediction window. The model demonstrated an AUROC of 0.861 (95% CI 0.856-0.867) and AUPRC of 0.771. The Brier score was 0.147, indicating slight overestimations of mortality risk. Explanatory diagrams utilizing SHAP values allowed visualization of feature impacts on predictions at both the global and individual levels.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Our machine learning model demonstrated good discrimination and precision-recall in predicting 365-day mortality risk among individuals with advanced cancer. It has the potential to provide personalized mortality predictions and facilitate earlier integration of palliative care.</AbstractText>

title: Explainable AI for infection prevention and control: modeling CPE acquisition and patient outcomes in an Irish hospital with transformers.
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Carbapenemase-Producing Enterobacteriace (CPE) poses a critical concern for infection prevention and control in hospitals. However, predictive modeling of previously highlighted CPE-associated risks such as readmission, mortality, and extended length of stay (LOS) remains underexplored, particularly with modern deep learning approaches. This study introduces an eXplainable AI (XAI) modeling framework to investigate CPE impact on patient outcomes from Electronic Medical Records (EMR) data of an Irish hospital.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">We analyzed an inpatient dataset from an Irish acute hospital (2018-2022), incorporating diagnostic codes, ward transitions, patient demographics, infection-related variables and contact network features. Several Transformer-based architectures (e.g., TabTransformer, TabNet) were benchmarked alongside traditional machine learning models. Clinical outcomes were predicted, and XAI techniques were applied to interpret model decisions.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Our framework successfully demonstrated the utility of Transformer-based models, with TabTransformer consistently outperforming baselines across multiple clinical prediction tasks, especially for CPE acquisition (Area Under Receiver Operating Characteristic and sensitivity). We found infection-related features, including historical hospital exposure, admission context, and network centrality measures, to be highly influential in predicting patient outcomes and CPE acquisition risk. Explainability analyses revealed that features like "Area of Residence", "Admission Ward" and prior admissions are key risk factors. Network variables like "Ward PageRank" also ranked highly, reflecting the potential value of structural exposure information.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">This study presents a robust and explainable AI framework for analyzing complex EMR data to identify key risk factors and predict CPE-related outcomes. Our findings underscore the superior performance of the Transformer models and highlight the importance of diverse clinical and network features. The transparent interpretability offered by our XAI approach provides actionable insights for infection prevention and control, paving the way for more targeted interventions and ultimately enhancing patient safety within acute healthcare settings.</AbstractText>

title: A prompt framework for enhancing LLM-based explainability of medical machine learning models: an intensive care unit application.
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) techniques like SHAP provide valuable insights into machine learning model predictions by quantifying feature contributions. However, interpreting these quantitative outputs remains unintuitive for many clinicians, hindering their practical adoption in clinical decision-making. This exploratory feasibility study aims to propose and evaluate a prompting framework designed to guide large language models (LLMs) in generating consistent, clinically relevant explanations from SHAP values. We developed a structured zero-shot prompting framework incorporating variable definitions, safety principles, and a three-step reasoning process; (1) key risk factors, (2) prediction-outcome reconciliation, (3) clinical recommendations. This framework guided GPT-4 to explain SHAP-based predictions from an ICU extubation failure model (trained on MIMIC-III data). The framework’s performance was assessed using quantitative consistency metrics (entropy, accuracy) and a qualitative clinician survey (n = 7). The LLM achieved a fidelity of 0.783 and entropy of 0.226, indicating consistent structured reasoning. On a 5-point Likert scale, clinicians rated the LLM-generated explanations as helpful (mean: 3.94 ± 0.48) and safe (4.21 ± 0.68). However, critical care specialists assigned lower scores than non-critical care physicians (helpfulness: 3.48 vs. 4.29; safety: 3.45 vs. 4.79), suggesting domain-specific caution in perceived utility. A structured prompting framework shows feasibility in leveraging LLMs to enhance the clinical interpretability of SHAP explanations. This methodological approach warrants further investigation and refinement for broader clinical application.

title: Machine learning and artificial intelligence for delirium prediction with Electronic Health Records (EHR): a scoping review.
abstract: Delirium, an acute and fluctuating neurocognitive disorder prevalent among hospitalized and geriatric surgical patients, remains a pervasive yet underrecognized clinical challenge. Leveraging Electronic Health Records (EHRs), Machine Learning (ML) models have emerged as promising tools for early prediction and intervention. This scoping review synthesizes the existing literature, identifies current research gaps, and outlines future directions to advance delirium prediction modeling. Following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, literature from 2020 to 2025 was systematically searched across Google Scholar, EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using a comprehensive query strategy. The review highlights a significant reliance on structured preoperative and intraoperative EHR for delirium prediction, despite the existence of abundant and highly informative unstructured clinical narratives. Furthermore, a substantial heterogeneity exists in the utilized delirium identification methodologies (e.g. Nursing Delirium Screening Scale (Nu-DESC), Delirium Observation Screening Scale (DOSS), International Classification of Diseases (ICD) criteria, 4AT delirium detection, Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC), Cornell Assessment of Pediatric Delirium (CAPD) Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th version (DSM-5), natural language processing (NLP) based analysis), alongside a focus on specific surgical subgroups. This limited data utilization and methodological variation pose challenges to ML model generalizability and robustness. The literature also showed a research emphasis on critically ill patients, potentially overlooking subtle delirium in low-severity cases. Future research should focus on early risk stratification and prioritize four key areas: (1) expanded utilization of both tabular EHR and unstructured clinical notes; (2) development of integrated multimodal fusion models adaptable to dynamic patient states; (3) investigation of the temporal dynamics of delirium development using time-series analysis; and (4) application of causal inference methods to elucidate the relationships between risk factors and delirium. Superior prediction performance can be achieved by leveraging cutting-edge architectures (e.g. transformers) and parallel computing efficiencies to move beyond traditional machine learning. To enhance real-world adoption, future work should integrate Explainable AI tools such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) within EHR-based decision support systems, improving interpretability and mitigating subgroup disparities in localized risk assessment.

title: Research trends and ethical perspectives on explainable artificial intelligence in emergency medicine: a bibliometric analysis.
abstract:
<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has become increasingly relevant for ensuring transparency, interpretability, and trust in clinical decision support systems. In emergency medicine, where decision-making is time-critical and data are often incomplete, XAI provides significant opportunities while also raising ethical and methodological challenges. Despite the rapid growth of AI applications in acute care, bibliometric studies explicitly integrating explainability and ethics remain limited.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A bibliometric analysis of 433 publications on XAI in emergency medicine was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection. The search covered 1986 through November 2025 and included peer-reviewed research articles and reviews in English related to emergency medicine, artificial intelligence, explainability, and ethics. Bibliometric indicators (publication trends, citation counts, journals, authors, and countries) were analyzed using Bibliometrix (R), while VOSviewer was used to visualize thematic clusters and keyword co-occurrence. Citations were analyzed as cumulative counts up to November 2025 and normalized to per-publication counts per year.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Research output increased sharply after 2018, peaking in 2023 with approximately 90 publications, reflecting the growing focus on interpretability and transparency in emergency care. Cumulative citations exceeded 1,400 by 2025. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China were the most productive countries. Annals of Emergency Medicine, NPJ Digital Medicine, and BMJ Open were the most influential journals, while Ong M.E.H., Dwivedi G., Stewart J., Wang Y., and Li J. emerged as leading contributors. Thematic mapping revealed four major clusters: (1) methodological development of interpretable models, (2) clinical applications in triage, imaging, and sepsis risk prediction, (3) ethical and human-factor dimensions (bias, accountability, transparency), and (4) emerging topics such as large language models. Despite rapid progress, most studies remained retrospective and lacked standardized interpretability metrics, multicenter validation, and consistent reporting of explainability outputs.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Research on XAI in emergency medicine is expanding rapidly and is increasingly shaped by a small group of influential journals and authors. However, critical gaps remain, including the limited availability of prospective studies, insufficient clinician involvement, and ethical frameworks that are not yet fully tailored to emergency settings. Addressing these gaps through multidisciplinary collaboration, standardized evaluation metrics, and stronger governance will be important to support transparency, accountability, and the safe clinical adoption of XAI in emergency medicine.</AbstractText>

<AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has become increasingly relevant for ensuring transparency, interpretability, and trust in clinical decision support systems. In emergency medicine, where decision-making is time-critical and data are often incomplete, XAI provides significant opportunities while also raising ethical and methodological challenges. Despite the rapid growth of AI applications in acute care, bibliometric studies explicitly integrating explainability and ethics remain limited.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A bibliometric analysis of 433 publications on XAI in emergency medicine was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection. The search covered 1986 through November 2025 and included peer-reviewed research articles and reviews in English related to emergency medicine, artificial intelligence, explainability, and ethics. Bibliometric indicators (publication trends, citation counts, journals, authors, and countries) were analyzed using Bibliometrix (R), while VOSviewer was used to visualize thematic clusters and keyword co-occurrence. Citations were analyzed as cumulative counts up to November 2025 and normalized to per-publication counts per year.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Research output increased sharply after 2018, peaking in 2023 with approximately 90 publications, reflecting the growing focus on interpretability and transparency in emergency care. Cumulative citations exceeded 1,400 by 2025. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China were the most productive countries. Annals of Emergency Medicine, NPJ Digital Medicine, and BMJ Open were the most influential journals, while Ong M.E.H., Dwivedi G., Stewart J., Wang Y., and Li J. emerged as leading contributors. Thematic mapping revealed four major clusters: (1) methodological development of interpretable models, (2) clinical applications in triage, imaging, and sepsis risk prediction, (3) ethical and human-factor dimensions (bias, accountability, transparency), and (4) emerging topics such as large language models. Despite rapid progress, most studies remained retrospective and lacked standardized interpretability metrics, multicenter validation, and consistent reporting of explainability outputs.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">Research on XAI in emergency medicine is expanding rapidly and is increasingly shaped by a small group of influential journals and authors. However, critical gaps remain, including the limited availability of prospective studies, insufficient clinician involvement, and ethical frameworks that are not yet fully tailored to emergency settings. Addressing these gaps through multidisciplinary collaboration, standardized evaluation metrics, and stronger governance will be important to support transparency, accountability, and the safe clinical adoption of XAI in emergency medicine.</AbstractText>

title: Keeping AI in medicine and radiology within the framework of scientific method: measuring to close the epistemic gap.
abstract: The classical scientific method-systematic observation, question formulation, hypothesis construction, experimental testing, analysis (including rejection or refinement), conclusion, and transparent communicationstructures reliable inference in medicine, based on the long way of development of modern science.Contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) and, in particular, foundation/large language models, seem to be inverting this logical one-way order by proposing "end-to-end" systems and supplying post hoc rationales.We argue that this "black-box acceleration" risks erasing intermediate epistemic steps unless development and evaluation are explicitly re-embedded in the workflow."Explainable" AI does not guarantee recovery of reasoning because of an epistemic gap: explanations are constrained to human clinical concepts even when a model's decision basis may be non-human yet causally valid, non-human and spurious, or human-readable but only post hoc.Of note, medical imaging AI studies show saliency instability, shortcut learning, and distributional fragility, especially when a system is translated to new/unknown contexts.Training and validating systems on the deployment population within a defined technical context reduces domain mismatch and improves calibration but can entrench local biases and impair portability to other populations or different technology systems.We herein propose a model of institutional AI program-hospital-embedded pipelines with auditable provenance, preregistered evaluations, task-grounded tests of causal alignment and invariance, publication of failures, and local-plus-external validation-to preserve the stepwise logic of science while accepting practical opacity.Finally, the detection of failures of AI systems is not only an ethical duty but also a way to improve the systems' performance and be considered for negotiations between AI developers and medical centers.The described canonical sequence of the scientific method remains the core scaffold of biomedical investigation.Its historical lineage is well established: Galileo Galilei integrated measurement with controlled experiment and mathematical analysis [1]; Francis Bacon formalized inductive empiricism [2]; Ren Descartes emphasized methodological doubt and structured reasoning [3]; Isaac Newton operationalized a hypothetic-deductive program with testable predictions grounded in mathematical laws [4].In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, medical science assimilated statistical design and causal inference through Pierre-Charles A. Louis's "numerical method" [5], Ronald A. Fisher's experimental design [6], Austin Bradford Hill's randomized trials and causality criteria [7], and Archibald L. Cochrane's insistence on effectiveness and efficiency in health services research [8].Karl R. Popper's falsificationism reframed scientific progress as the survival of hypotheses under attempted refutation [9].The theoryleadenness of observation-as emphasized by Norwood R. Hanson [10] and later by Thomas S. Kuhn [11]-shows that data are interpreted through conceptual lenses.This insight does not entail epistemic relativism, but it does demand explicit models and reproducible tests that can be scrutinized and challenged across competing paradigms.

title: Fate-tox: fragment attention transformer for E(3)-equivariant multi-organ toxicity prediction.
abstract: Toxicity is a critical hurdle in drug development, often causing the late-stage failure of promising compounds. Existing computational prediction models often focus on single-organ toxicity. However, avoiding toxicity of an organ, such as reducing gastrointestinal side effects, may inadvertently lead to toxicity in another organ, as seen in the real case of rofecoxib, which was withdrawn due to increased cardiovascular risks. Thus, simultaneous prediction of multi-organ toxicity is a desirable but challenging task. The main challenges are (1) the variability of substructures that contribute to toxicity of different organs, (2) insufficient power of molecular representations in diverse perspectives, and (3) explainability of prediction results especially in terms of substructures or potential toxicophores. To address these challenges with multiple strategies, we developed FATE-Tox, a novel multi-view deep learning framework for multi-organ toxicity prediction. For variability of substructures, we used three fragmentation methods such as BRICS, Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and RDKit Functional Groups to formulate fragment-level graphs so that diverse substructures can be used to identify toxicity for different organs. For insufficient power of molecular representations, we used molecular representations in both 2D and 3D perspectives. For explainability, our fragment attention transformer identifies potential 3D toxicophores using attention coefficients. Scientific contribution: Our framework achieved significant improvements in prediction performance, with up to 3.01% gains over prior baseline methods on toxicity benchmark datasets from MoleculeNet (BBBP, SIDER, ClinTox) and TDC (DILI, Skin Reaction, Carcinogens, and hERG), while the multi-task learning approach further enhanced performance by up to 1.44% compared to the single-task learning framework that had already surpassed these baselines. Additionally, attention visualization aligning with literature contributes to greater transparency in predictive modeling. Our approach has the potential to provide scientists and clinicians with a more interpretable and clinically meaningful tool to assess systemic toxicity, ultimately supporting safer and more informed drug development processes.

abstract:
<AbstractText Label="PURPOSE">Early detection of brain metastases (BMs) is critical for prompt treatment and optimal control of the disease. In this study, we seek to predict the risk of developing BM among patients diagnosed with lung cancer on the basis of electronic health record (EHR) data and to understand what factors are important for the model to predict BM development through explainable artificial intelligence approaches accurately.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="MATERIALS AND METHODS">We trained a recurrent neural network model, REverse Time AttentIoN (RETAIN), to predict the risk of developing BM using structured EHR data. To interpret the model's decision process, we analyzed the attention weights in the RETAIN model and the SHAP values from a feature attribution method, Kernel SHAP, to identify the factors contributing to BM prediction.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="RESULTS">We developed a high-quality cohort with 4,466 patients with BM from the Cerner Health Fact database, which contains over 70 million patients from more than 600 hospitals. RETAIN uses this data set to achieve the best area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at 0.825, a significant improvement over the baseline model. We also extended a feature attribution method, Kernel SHAP, to structured EHR data for model interpretation. Both RETAIN and Kernel SHAP can identify important features related to BM prediction.</AbstractText>
          <AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION">To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to predict BM using structured EHR data. We achieved decent prediction performance for BM prediction and identified factors highly relevant to BM development. The sensitivity analysis demonstrated that both RETAIN and Kernel SHAP could discriminate unrelated features and put more weight on the features important to BM. Our study explored the potential of applying explainable artificial intelligence for future clinical applications.</AbstractText>

title: Why Didn't Nietzsche Get His Act Together?
abstract: Although Elijah Millgram identifies analytic philosophers as his “tribe,” he doesn’t have much use for the analytically competent work that has sparked the widely recognized improvement of Nietzsche scholarship over the last several decades. Such work, he complains, tends not to recognize that Nietzsche “writes funny” (2). It reads him “straight,” reconstructing his books on the “deeply misguided” assumption that he actually had views or beliefs. Actually, almost all important Nietzsche scholars of recent vintage recognize that Nietzsche doesn’t write like the typical philosopher, giving straightforward arguments for clearly marked positions. And they usually offer an explanation. Millgram’s explanation is certainly new: Nietzsche doesn’t write in the standard way because he couldn’t, for the same reason that he couldn’t get his act together. He is a decadent, a disunified agent “coming apart at the seams,” whose apparent beliefs do not count as such because they are not the expressions of an integrated person. Yet what emerged from his disintegration was the brilliant way of writing philosophy exhibited in his later books. The way to read them, Millgram claims, extending Alexander Nehamas’s reading of Beyond Good and Evil (hereafter BGE), is to ask “who their authors are” (39). He finds a different author for each book, a different voice or perspective, each exhibiting a different side of the agent that Nietzsche could not pull together: the genealogist or intellectual in Genealogy (hereafter GM), the good European in BGE, the convalescent in The Gay Science (hereafter GS), the psychologist in Twilight of the Idols (hereafter TI), and so on. This sounds interesting, even exciting, and it might have been if Millgram had made much of a case for his way of reading Nietzsche.It is hardly news that Nietzsche did fall apart, collapsing in early 1890 and spending the last ten years of his life insane. It would not be surprising if books finished shortly before his collapse showed signs of the impending disaster. And they do, it seems to us. The works of 1888, including TI, present their ideas more straightforwardly and even crudely compared to BGE (1886) and GM (1887), which exhibit a tremendous power to organize complex ideas in artistic and subtle ways. And it’s possible that we may find in the 1888 books what Millgram calls “blurts,” words that are not under Nietzsche’s control but are simply blurted out. The question is whether these are unfortunate effects of Nietzsche’s degeneration, as we are inclined to think, or essential aspects of the philosophy he was doing in his later books, as Millgram claims. The evidence he presents for his view is that the same kind of blurts are found in GM and BGE. This is the crucial claim on which the plausibility of his whole interpretation rests.Millgram takes three elements from BGE—its theory of the soul as a collection of drives that may or may not be united into a fully integrated agent, its claim that Europeans are not fully integrated, and the occurrence of extended blurts in the text—from which he infers that BGE is presenting its author, “the good European,” as “a field of unregimented, quasi-independent drives successively seizing control of him for the duration of one or another ranting diatribe.” These rants express “misogynistic, antisemitic, and nationalistic excesses” that the good European goes on to disavow “on the elaborately theorized grounds that this personality was unable to anchor the full-fledged attribution of opinions, choices, and attitudes generally” (256–57). This is nonsense. First, the so-called diatribes do not read like rants. With the exception of the remarks on women, there is no vitriol in them, and they seem very much under Nietzsche’s control. But it does take some work to read them. The nationalistic “diatribe” begins with an over-the-top ode to Wagner’s overture to Meistersinger, but then changes tone, saying of Wagner’s overture, “no beauty, nothing of the south or of the southerly brightness of sky, nothing of gracefulness, no dance, hardly any will to logic” (Nietzsche [1886] 2003: 240). For anyone who knows Nietzsche’s views on music, this is clearly in Nietzsche’s own voice. It tells us what he wants from music and what Wagner’s music lacks. Contrary to Millgram’s reading, Nietzsche is referring not to this statement when he goes on to say “I have just given an example” of the “hearty fatherlandishness” that good Europeans may sometimes “permit themselves” for short periods, but only to the ode. Second, Nietzsche ([1886] 2003: 241) explicitly presents the ode’s nationalism as a “lapse into old loves and narrowness” and identifies overcoming “such atavistic attacks” as a “return to reason, that is to say, to good Europeanism.” So good Europeans may permit themselves patriotic feelings for a short period of time (think of cheering for one’s country at the Olympic Games), but only the overcoming of such narrow and outmoded feelings makes them good Europeans. Third, issues regarding unity and attributability (Millgram’s obsession, not Nietzsche’s) have nothing to do with Nietzsche’s disavowal of fatherlandishness. Rather, he is showing us what must be overcome to be a good European. In a good European patriotism is not an “unregimented” drive but rather a feeling that is “permitted” occasionally but has been put in its place. And it is perhaps a necessary feeling. If you don’t love your country, how are you going to learn to love less narrow communities?The so-called anti-Semitic tirade is even harder to read because instead of offering its perspectives consecutively, it goes back and forth between the one Nietzsche disavows and his own, making it impossible to discern which is which without carefully examining the content. Millgram doesn’t bother, finding the content “uninteresting” and “almost” what “you could have heard in pretty much any pub in Germany or Austro-Hungary” at the time. This is almost dishonest. Only in a footnote does Millgram explain the “almost,” acknowledging the suggestion at the end of Nietzsche “diatribe” that “it would perhaps be a good idea to eject the antisemitic ranters from the country” (251). That should certainly have led him to examine the content carefully to sort out the perspectives and see if it is really either anti-Semitic or a diatribe.BGE’s alleged misogynistic remarks are the only ones that even sound like a rant. One of us has written about this issue, arguing that these remarks are directed against “woman,” the social construction of womanhood (which a passage in GS [Nietzsche [1882/1887] 1974: 68] blames on men), and not against individual women who may not exemplify it (Clark 1994, 2015). Millgram lauds Clark’s article and accepts its view that the way Nietzsche frames his remarks suggest that they do not represent his beliefs about women but only his sentiments (302). But he disagrees with Clark’s view that Nietzsche is showing us how he overcame misogynist beliefs, even if some of the corresponding sentiments may remain. However, he does not acknowledge Clark’s argument (which is based on the wider framing of the relevant remarks, their presence in a chapter titled “Our Virtues,” and that chapter’s contents), much less provide any reason against it. He merely reiterates his account of Nietzsche’s alleged nationalistic and anti-Semitic rants. This might have some force if he had made plausible his account of these “rants,” but we have shown that he does not. In fact it is striking how unlike these “rants” his misogynistic comments are in tone and how difficult it is to see that Nietzsche’s own perspective differs from the one he disavows. It is as if Nietzsche is letting us know that he is still dealing with these feelings, unlike the nationalism and anti-Semitism he is way beyond.There is still hope for Millgram’s interpretation in his account of the author of GM as “prone to emotional outbursts that induced sudden swerves in his train of thought, and which made him unable to remain consistent over even short stretches of text” (256). That account provides the most detailed textual support for Millgram’s overall interpretation, and he appeals to it repeatedly to bolster weak interpretations of other books and to brush off any suggestion that Nietzsche’s “blurts” might be merely unfortunate effects of his impending collapse. If this account is plausible, we might grant that he needs weaker evidence for his account of the BGE “diatribes.” But it is not. Millgram’s claim is that Nietzsche obviously contradicts himself in GM; he is “standing up, waving a large, brightly colored flag, and practically shouting to the skies, ‘I am contradicting myself’” (17). The contradiction is supposed to be this: Nietzsche criticizes a theory on the grounds that forgetting is a lot harder than the theory supposes. Later, however, he claims that forgetting is the normal state for humans, so that severe punishment was required to “create a memory” in them. He even argues that forgetting is so easy that those who invented hell forgot that they invented it! And then “he rubs it in by later referring back to the discussion of his predecessors: ‘To say it again—or haven’t I said it yet? [i.e., I’ve already forgotten]—they are worthless’ (5:297/GM 2.4). And why worthless? Because they’ve forgotten the history of morality” (16). This is a terrible reading of the text.Nietzsche’s initial point about the difficulty of forgetting is directed against the “English psychologists,” those whose philosophical psychology is rooted in British empiricism. He sees them as trying to explain how human beings came to the idea that human qualities can be good in themselves, as opposed to simply useful or good for oneself. Kant’s account of the good will and the categorical imperative provides an answer, but he is no English psychologist; he is not attempting to fit morality into naturalistic picture of the world. Hume is trying to do so and therefore has a different answer, roughly that empathy moves us from an egoistic to a common perspective. Nietzsche does not accept either answer, but does not offer his objections when considering the answer of his naturalistic predecessors. This is because, apparently unbeknownst to Millgram, the predecessor he is most interested in is his own earlier self. He is criticizing and correcting his own theory from nine years earlier: that “one begins by calling actions good or bad … solely on account of their useful or harmful consequences” for oneself or those one cares about. “Soon, however, one forgets the origins of these designations and believes that the quality ‘good’ or ‘bad’ is inherent in the objects themselves” ([1878] 1996: 39). He criticizes his earlier view on multiple grounds, including the “psychological absurdity” of supposing that people come to consider a quality or resulting action good in itself (a virtue or virtuous action) simply by forgetting that they value it because of its usefulness to them, a “usefulness [that] has been the everyday experience in all ages, something therefore that was continually underscored anew; accordingly … could not help but impress itself upon consciousness with ever greater clarity” ([1887] 1998: I: 3). It is like explaining people’s pursuit of money as if it were good in itself by saying that they simply forget that they value it for what it can buy.Nietzsche’s criticism of his earlier and simplistic account in no way commits him to holding that forgetting is in general or always hard. It therefore in no way contradicts the claim that humans are naturally forgetful, by which he means that many of our mental processes are kept out of consciousness and that this is required for health. Nietzsche alleges forgetfulness made punishment necessary in order to keep five or six “I will nots” in consciousness. The problem was never that humans forgot what it was in their own interest to remember (and that may not even have required consciousness) but that they had a hard time remembering—or caring about—what was in the community interest. That’s why it was necessary to create a memory in them. Millgram rightly points out, as if it is a problem, that this “creation of a memory” presupposes the existence of memory. If you are not already able to remember the pain it causes, punishment can’t teach you to remember anything. But Nietzsche is talking about a specific kind of memory here, what he calls “a memory of the will,” a memory of promises one has made. That one must already have the kind of memory animals have in order to develop a memory of commitments in no way contradicts GM’s original claim regarding the psychological absurdity of arriving at the idea of something being good in itself by forgetting that one calls things “good” to indicate that they serve one’s own interests.Consider now Millgram’s claim that Nietzsche uses the ease of forgetting to make it seem plausible that slaves invented the idea of hell to get revenge against the nobles who were oppressing them. “But if the slaves have invented their revenge,” Millgram objects, “why don’t they know it’s imaginary? And if they do, how can they find it satisfying? The account only makes sense if the slaves have forgotten.” But Nietzsche never says that the slaves invent hell for the purpose of getting revenge against the masters. Millgram seems to picture the slaves sitting around wondering how to get revenge on the nobles until someone says, “I know, why don’t we invent the idea of hell and its everlasting torments?” To the extent that Nietzsche thinks the slave invented the idea of hell, the point is that their ressentiment against the nobles attracted them to believing in a place after death, the idea of which had been in place for some time and which was developed into a place of punishment by resentful priests. There is no reason to take Nietzsche to hold that the priests, much less the slaves, were ever aware of why they believed in hell, and so no reason to think they forgot. So none of this shows anything like an obvious contradiction. Perhaps Millgram’s best argument for his claim about Nietzsche’s forgetfulness concerns Nietzsche’s evidently throwaway line: “to say it again, or haven’t I said it yet?” Millgram may be right that Nietzsche is indicating that he is being forgetful, but that is completely consistent with his theory. Further, he may be alerting us to a distinction between forgetting what you said and forgetting what you think. Nietzsche knows what he thought, but wonders if he said it. Is that really the sign of a personality falling apart, or a prompt to figure out the different kinds of forgetting Nietzsche is talking about?Millgram has one final card, which is his attack on the Principle of Charity (POC). He would undoubtedly charge that our “smoothing out” of the contradictions in GM is made possible only by our acceptance of the POC, which “requires you not to impute contradictions to a text whenever that is at all avoidable” (24). Although “philosophers are trained to apply and invoke the Principle,” Millgram claims that they don’t know why; “if you ask almost any professional philosopher for a justification, you’ll get reiterated insistence, but not an argument.” And so he chastises his analytic colleagues: “We shouldn’t apply the methods we were taught in graduate school merely by reflex.” When Millgram courageously breaks from his tribe to ask, “Why be charitable?” he discovers that charity was “originally … warranted by a feature of the text [the Bible] that made it appropriate, namely, its divine authorship.” Likewise, his reading of Nietzsche’s texts is warranted by a feature of these texts, that they are constructed “to exhibit the tendency of a personality type to inconsistency.” But since such texts “should be expected to exhibit inconsistencies,” this makes objecting to an interpretation on the basis of Charity “a mistake.” In the case of Nietzsche’s texts, “bracketing the Principle is no more than respect for the text in front of us” (25). We are of course applying a modified version of the POC in our interpretation of GM. As with any interpretation, one must aim to make the most sense of what the author is claiming, and that cannot be done if one leaves simply leaves apparent contradictions in place without considering how they might be resolved. Millgram’s own interpretation of GM is based on the same modified version of the POC that we apply, in its implication that it makes no sense for Nietzsche to say the things he does unless he is trying to show us that he is contradicting himself. Are we supposed to simply take his word for this, or are we allowed to consider whether it actually makes the most sense of what Nietzsche says in GM? We have argued that it doesn’t even come close.We end on a note of agreement with Millgram’s evaluation of Nietzsche as “an impressive figure, a deep and powerful philosopher, and someone that you have to take completely seriously, even when you’re not about to sign onto one or another view or program. You owe it to yourself, as a philosopher, to think his ideas through, and more often than not, my own experience has it, doing so will change your mind about something you had thought was a settled matter” (263). We just wish his book had provided much evidence for this evaluation.
